[{:db/id 17592186055121 :question/problem "A solution to the linear equation $y=3x-2$ is the ordered pair $(4,t).$ What is the value of $t?$" :question/worked-solution "Since $(4,t)$ is a solution to the linear equation $y=3x-2,$ the equation must turn into a true statement if we substitute $4$ and $t$ for $x$ and $y.$ So, we replace $x$ with $4$ and $y$ with $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x-2 \\ (t) & =3(4)-2 \\ t & =12-2 \\ t & =10\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186052094 :answer-field/correct 17592186052095 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186054693 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8850735f-3807-552e-a696-83fed33439b4"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-8850735f-3807-552e-a696-83fed33439b4" :question/id #uuid "8850735f-3807-552e-a696-83fed33439b4" :question/math-academy-id "q-44331" :question/problem "Which of the following ordered pairs is **NOT** a solution to $y=3x+4?$

I. $(4,16)$

II. $(0,4)$

III. $(3,12)$" :question/worked-solution "To check whether each point is a solution to the equation, we substitute it into the equation and see if it results in a true statement.

First, we substitute $(4,16)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x+4 \\ (16) & =3(4)+4 \\ 16 & =12+4 \\ 16 & =16\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

The result is a true statement, so $(4,16)$ is a solution to the equation.

Next, we substitute $(0,4)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x+4 \\ (4) & =3(0)+4 \\ 4 & =4\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

The result is again a true statement, so $(0,4)$ is also a solution to the equation.

Finally, we substitute $(3,12)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x+4 \\ (12) & =3(3)+4 \\ 12 & =9+4 \\ 12 & =13\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

The result is a false statement, so $(3,12)$ is *not* a solution to the equation.

So, out of the three ordered pairs given, the only pair that is *not* a solution to the equation is III $(3,12).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b78c8c28-e7f5-5c67-a2f4-7acc6b4dc795"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b78c8c28-e7f5-5c67-a2f4-7acc6b4dc795" :answer-field/id #uuid "b78c8c28-e7f5-5c67-a2f4-7acc6b4dc795" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-03a6c279-2e8a-5668-8055-0c5048d986d9" :answer-field/choices ["answer-55cd2295-7391-5333-b505-2bebeab49eda" "answer-c46fb7a0-b425-5c37-9b0c-bf407dbdefee" "answer-c8246af6-e321-5c32-9d54-0be845fb1a81" "answer-ee218eec-e653-595b-ae8d-c1cb3b786e4e" "answer-03a6c279-2e8a-5668-8055-0c5048d986d9"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-55cd2295-7391-5333-b505-2bebeab49eda" :answer/id #uuid "55cd2295-7391-5333-b505-2bebeab49eda" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c46fb7a0-b425-5c37-9b0c-bf407dbdefee" :answer/id #uuid "c46fb7a0-b425-5c37-9b0c-bf407dbdefee" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c8246af6-e321-5c32-9d54-0be845fb1a81" :answer/id #uuid "c8246af6-e321-5c32-9d54-0be845fb1a81" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ee218eec-e653-595b-ae8d-c1cb3b786e4e" :answer/id #uuid "ee218eec-e653-595b-ae8d-c1cb3b786e4e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-03a6c279-2e8a-5668-8055-0c5048d986d9" :answer/id #uuid "03a6c279-2e8a-5668-8055-0c5048d986d9" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186055294 :question/problem "Which of the following ordered pairs is **NOT** a solution to $y=\frac{x}{4}?$

I. $(-8,-2)$

II. $(4,1)$

III. $(-4,1)$" :question/worked-solution "To check whether each point is a solution to the equation, we substitute it into the equation and see if it results in a true statement.

First, we substitute $(-8,-2)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{4} \\ (-2) & =\frac{-8}{4} \\ -2 & =-2\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

The result is a true statement, so $(-8,-2)$ is a solution to the equation.

Next, we substitute $(4,1)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{4} \\ (1) & =\frac{4}{4} \\ 1 & =1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

The result is again a true statement, so $(4,1)$ is also a solution to the equation.

Finally, we substitute $(-4,1)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{4} \\ (1) & =\frac{-4}{4} \\ 1 & =-1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

The result is a false statement, so $(-4,1)$ is *not* a solution to the equation.

So, out of the three ordered pairs given, the only pair that is *not* a solution to the equation is III $(-4,1).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+3L\{1\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=-L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+3L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}

Now, solving the first equation for ${X}_{1}(s),$ we get

Substituting this in the second equation and solving for ${X}_{2}(s),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{2}(s)-1 & =-{X}_{1}(s)+3{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s-3){X}_{2}(s) & =1-{X}_{1}(s) \\ (s-3){X}_{2}(s) & =1-(\frac{3-2s}{s(s-1)}) \\ (s-3){X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{s(s-1)-3+2s}{s(s-1)} \\ (s-3){X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}-s-3+2s}{s(s-1)} \\ (s-3){X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}+s-3}{s(s-1)} \\ {X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{{s}^{2}+s-3}{s(s-1)(s-3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution of the new system  in terms of parameter $s$ is 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=\frac{3-2s}{s(s-1)},\,{X}_{2}(s)=\frac{{s}^{2}+s-3}{s(s-1)(s-3)}.

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform $L$ to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a system with variables ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}.$ In terms of the parameter $s,$ the solution of the new system is

${X}_{2}(s)=\frac{s+2}{s(s-5)}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{2{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t)\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{5{x}_{2}(t)+2\}\end{aligned}\,\,
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+3L\{{x}_{2}(t)\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=5L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}+2L\{1\}\end{aligned}
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-0=2{X}_{1}(s)+3{X}_{2}(s) \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-1=5{X}_{2}(s)+\frac{2}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\},$ and we have used the fact that $L\{1\}=\frac{1}{s}.$

Now, solving the second equation for ${X}_{2}(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{2}(s)-1 & =5{X}_{2}(s)+\frac{2}{s} \\ (s-5){X}_{2}(s) & =1+\frac{2}{s} \\ (s-5){X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{s+2}{s} \\ {X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{s+2}{s(s-5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this in the first equation and solving for ${X}_{1}(s)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s) & =2{X}_{1}(s)+3{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s-2){X}_{1}(s) & =3{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s-2){X}_{1}(s) & =3(\frac{s+2}{s(s-5)}) \\ {X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{3(s+2)}{s(s-5)(s-2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution of the new system in terms of parameter $s$ is 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=\frac{3(s+2)}{s(s-2)(s-5)},\,{X}_{2}(s)=\frac{s+2}{s(s-5)}.

$$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2x+7,\, & x\le 1 \\ 2x-3,\, & x>1\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since $x=1$ is in the interval $x\le 1,$ we use the left-hand branch, namely $f(x)=2x+7:$

What is the definition of the function $y=f(x)$ shown above?" :question/worked-solution "We will graph each branch separately.

- On the interval $(-\infty ,1],$ we have a line with slope $2$ and $y$-intercept $1.$ So the graph is the line $y=2x+1$ that ends at $(1,3),$ including this point.

- On the interval $(1,\infty )$, we have a line with a slope of $-2$ that passes through the point $(1,0).$ We can find the equation of this line using point-slope form:

$$
y-0=-2(x-1)\,⟹\,y=2-2x
$$

So the graph is the line $y=2-2x$ that starts at $(1,0),$ excluding this point.

Therefore, the function is defined as follows:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2x+1,\, & x\le 1 \\ 2-2x,\, & x>1\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186057606 :answer-field/correct "answer-e56d03f3-6214-5a2d-b812-62eb1213aa8f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e6676b49-b44c-580f-b15e-a5e689da79a6" "answer-0df10c74-c1ce-5a90-98c4-8fba09a65fd5" "answer-e56d03f3-6214-5a2d-b812-62eb1213aa8f" "answer-dfa718ca-5e40-5093-8ed6-1a6926b999dd"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e6676b49-b44c-580f-b15e-a5e689da79a6" :answer/id #uuid "e6676b49-b44c-580f-b15e-a5e689da79a6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}1-x,\, & x\le 1 \\ x-1,\, & x>1\end{aligned}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0df10c74-c1ce-5a90-98c4-8fba09a65fd5" :answer/id #uuid "0df10c74-c1ce-5a90-98c4-8fba09a65fd5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2x+1,\, & x\le 1 \\ -2-2x,\, & x>1\end{aligned}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e56d03f3-6214-5a2d-b812-62eb1213aa8f" :answer/id #uuid "e56d03f3-6214-5a2d-b812-62eb1213aa8f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2x+1,\, & x\le 1 \\ 2-2x,\, & x>1\end{aligned}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dfa718ca-5e40-5093-8ed6-1a6926b999dd" :answer/id #uuid "dfa718ca-5e40-5093-8ed6-1a6926b999dd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2x-1,\, & x\le 1 \\ 1-2x,\, & x>1\end{aligned}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186060275 :question/worked-solution "The function is defined  for values less than $-1,$ and between $-1$ and $4.$

17592186192492 :question/problem "Represent the solution of the inequality $k -12 \lt  -5$ on a number line." :question/worked-solution "To isolate $k,$ we need to perform the *opposite* of *subtracting* $12,$ which is *adding* $12.$

$$
\begin{aligned}k-12 & <-5 \\ k-12+12 & <-5+12 \\ k+0 & <7 \\ k & <7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $k \lt  7.$ The solution can be expressed on a number line, as shown below.

![](images/9c/9cc25f8eec7586ce65a17be3eb7af6ee509d014bf8dc9896cd45c6ef99769250.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192748 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-70d3487e-b503-50e8-b857-c63dd534d65a" "question-5f4cf73b-e442-544c-845a-c7e6521bdf69"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192467 :question/worked-solution "The variable $a$ is being *multiplied* by $-6.$ To isolate $a,$ we can perform the *opposite* operation, which is *dividing* by $-6.$ So, we divide both sides of the equation by $-6.$

Remember, when multiplying or dividing by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6a\,\, & >\,\,-12 \\ \frac{-6a}{-6}\, & <\,\,\frac{-12}{-6} \\ \frac{-6a}{-6}\, & <\,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $-6$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-6a}{-6} & <2 \\ \frac{\cancel{-6}a}{\cancel{-6}} & <2 \\ a & <2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $a<   2.$ The solution can be expressed on a number line, as shown below.

![](images/2b/2b5947166eb517c08355c09c265f6a2c1f87bdafd776b2e03f5503585568b90b.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192746 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6280d0e4-77c7-572f-9c1a-10c2908c012a" "question-bd2c58ff-4c4c-5b74-8ac8-2ec07ff5ad46" "question-93f851d7-f3f4-511e-adef-c16fd42c2432"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192464 :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the addition principle, adding $6$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}14 & <5x-6 \\ 14+6 & <5x-6+6 \\ 20 & <5x+0 \\ 20 & <5x\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $5{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}20 & <5x \\ \frac{20}{5} & <\frac{5x}{5} \\ \frac{20}{5} & <\frac{\cancel{5}x}{\cancel{5}} \\ 4 & <x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, let's swap the left and right-hand sides so that the variable is on the left-hand side. Remember that we also need to flip the inequality.

$$
x \gt 4
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x  \gt 4.$ The solution can be expressed on a number line, as shown below.

Remember to perform the same operation on the right-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}a+5 & \ge 11 \\ a+5-5 & \ge 11-5 \\ a+0 & \ge 6 \\ a & \ge 6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $a\ge 6.$ The solution can be expressed on a number line, as shown below.

$$
\begin{aligned}5z & \le -45 \\ \frac{5z}{5} & \le \frac{-45}{5} \\ \frac{5z}{5} & \le -9\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $5$ from the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5z}{5} & \le -9 \\ \frac{\cancel{5}z}{\cancel{5}} & \le -9 \\ z & \le -9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $z\le -9.$ The solution can be expressed on a number line, as shown below.

inequality $-\frac{a}{4}>-2$ on a number line." :question/worked-solution "The variable $a$ is being *divided* by $4.$ To isolate $a$ and remove the negative sign, we *multiply* by $-4.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{a}{4}\,\, & >\,\,-2 \\ (-4)\cdot (-\frac{a}{4})\,\, & <\,\,(-4)\cdot (-2) \\ (-4)\cdot (-\frac{a}{4})\,\, & <\,\,8\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)\cdot (-\frac{a}{4}) & <8 \\ (\cancel{-}4)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{a}{4}) & <8 \\ 4\cdot \frac{a}{4} & <8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $4$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot \frac{a}{4} & <8 \\ \frac{4a}{4} & <8 \\ \frac{\cancel{4}a}{\cancel{4}} & <8 \\ a & <8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $a<8.$ The solution can be expressed on a number line, as shown below.

{:db/id 17592186193332 :question/problem "Represent the solution of the inequality $-3x+2\ge 5$ on a number line." :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $2$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+2 & \ge 5 \\ -3x+2-2 & \ge 5-2 \\ -3x+0 & \ge 3 \\ -3x & \ge 3\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing by $-3.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x\,\, & \ge \,\,3 \\ \frac{-3x}{-3}\, & \le \,\,\frac{3}{-3} \\ \frac{\cancel{-3}x}{\cancel{-3}}\, & \le \,\,-1 \\ x\,\, & \le \,\,-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\le -1.$ The solution can be expressed on a number line, as shown below.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & \le 8 \\ \frac{4x}{4} & \le \frac{8}{4} \\ \frac{\cancel{4}x}{\cancel{4}} & \le \frac{8}{4} \\ x & \le 2\end{aligned}

{:db/id 17592186193860 :tutorial/content "We can always represent the solution of an inequality using a number line.

For example, let's express the solution of the following inequality using a number line:

$$
5x \geq 30
$$

The variable $x$ is being *multiplied* by $5.$ To isolate $x,$ we can perform the *opposite* operation, which is *dividing* by $5.$ So, we divide both sides of the inequality by $5{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}5x & \ge 30 \\ \frac{5x}{5} & \ge \frac{30}{5} \\ \frac{5x}{5} & \ge 6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $5$ from the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5x}{5} & \ge 6 \\ \frac{\cancel{5}x}{\cancel{5}} & \ge 6 \\ x & \ge 6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x \geq 6.$ This solution can be expressed on a number line, as shown below.

![](images/c3/c3a3d5a89d9181af5de9658ad2ac00cd8026a3050d48765dba5f5b23d3a0e7bc.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192908 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186221431 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-90de09a4-cb73-52eb-bce8-60541ed9cd90"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186370079 :question/problem "For the function

$$
G(s)=\frac{6}{{s}^{5}},\,s>0
$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{6}{{s}^{5}}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{F(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{3!}{{s}^{3+1}}\} \\  & ={t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$, then

$$
L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{G(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{F(s)}{s}\} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{τ}^{3}\,\text{d}τ \\  & =\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-90de09a4-cb73-52eb-bce8-60541ed9cd90" :question/id #uuid "90de09a4-cb73-52eb-bce8-60541ed9cd90" :question/math-academy-id "q-330844" :question/problem "For the function

$$
G(s)=\frac{120}{{s}^{7}},\,s>0
$$

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{120}{{s}^{7}}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{120}{{s}^{6}}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{F(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{120}{{s}^{6}}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{5!}{{s}^{5+1}}\} \\  & ={t}^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$, then

$$
L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{G(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{F(s)}{s}\} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{τ}^{5}\,\text{d}τ \\  & =\frac{{t}^{6}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c608cf93-4730-5e85-9788-45b64178d3fb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Suppose the spinner is spun $21$ times. What is the variance of the number of times the spinner lands on blue?" :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times the spinner lands on blue.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=21$ trials

- the probability of landing on blue is

$$
p=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(21,\frac{1}{3}).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the variance is given by

$$
\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p),
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the variance of the number of times the spinner lands on blue is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =np(1-p) \\  & =21\cdot \frac{1}{3}\cdot (1-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =7\cdot \frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{14}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2db3a67a-7d60-5de0-94bb-64450c65d4fe"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id representation of the set $S=\{-2,2\}\times {N}_{0}$ in the Cartesian plane?" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=\{-2,2\}\times {N}_{0}
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is either $-2$ or $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is a natural number or zero.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in \{-2,2\},\,y\in {N}_{0}\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{-2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $-2$ and whose $y$-coordinate  is any natural number or zero.

$$
{S}_{-2}=\{(-2,y)\,:\,y\in {N}_{0}\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-2}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/44/4418001fb8fb44cc5cd35b258136ee696d35d27198549177a2f60a7297d31bb1.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate  is any natural number or zero.

$$
{S}_{2}=\{(2,y)\,:\,y\in {N}_{0}\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{2}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/bf/bf74df976235b72a24047e2ec27aad7d426b6ceb1fcb948bc656b77bf0635911.png)

Our Cartesian product $S$ is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={S}_{-2}\cup {S}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $\{-2,2\}\times {N}_{0}$ as the set of points in the diagram below.

17592186082947 :question/problem "Sketch the graph of $y=|x|-3$." :question/worked-solution "Remember that $y=|x|+a$ is a vertical translation of the absolute value graph $y=|x|$ by $a$ units up.

The function $y=|x|-3$ has $a=-3.$ Therefore, it is a vertical translation of the absolute value graph $y=|x|$ by $3$ units *down*.

![](images/72/7266634257d662b0af75fdb80d402acaa779df2ed4b62fc43c074a7f4f902de0.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083190 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-276e0cea-6920-5a35-bd19-e10e6d09e8ad"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186082948 :question/problem "Sketch the graph of $y=|x-3|$." :question/worked-solution "Remember that $y=|x-a|$ is a horizontal translation of the absolute value graph $y=|x|$ by $a$ units right.

The function $y=|x-3|$ has $a=3.$ Therefore, it is a horizontal translation of the absolute value graph $y=|x|$ by $3$ units right.

Which of the figures above is a rhombus?" :question/worked-solution "First, recall the hierarchy diagram of quadrilaterals, where each shape below another is a specific type of the one above it.

![](images/1d/1dbe4c3e8ea97c0ac077c37143802366c5817d86965ab1dbc5abf54cd01d27c3.png)

Remember that a rhombus is a parallelogram where all sides are congruent.

With that in mind, let's look at each shape in turn.

- The shape $P$ is a rectangle. The sides are not all congruent, so it is not a rhombus.

- The shape $Q$ is a square. All its sides are congruent and the opposite sides are parallel, so it is a rhombus.

- The shape $R$ is a trapezoid. Since it has only one pair of parallel sides, it is not a rhombus.

- The shape $S$ is an isosceles trapezoid.  Since it has only one pair of parallel sides, it is not a rhombus.

Therefore, shape $Q$ is a rhombus. The shapes $P,$ $R,$ and $S$ are not rhombuses." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7c39ae96-03b7-5d75-924b-50c66d2fd7a7"] :db/ensure "question-b9ab7545-6c81-5c20-9f25-5d780715f99d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064146 :question/problem "Consider the function $y = x^5 (\cos x)^x.$ Its derivative is given by

$$
y'(x) = x^4 (\cos x)^x \left( 5 + g(x) \right).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y = x^5 (\cos x)^x.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{5})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{5}{x}+(x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+x\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{5}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+x\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{5}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{5}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y = x^5 (\cos x)^x {:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}(\frac{5}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & ={x}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}(\frac{5}{x}+\frac{x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{x}-\frac{{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}(5+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(x) = x \ln ( \cos  x ) - x^2 \tan x.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064310 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8a442047-ed6e-5bb4-89b9-beaee4b1e553" "question-adde1803-10ec-5c3d-8c04-d7e2c5d99587" "question-310e9298-b624-54d9-ac03-bed77b7fdecc" "question-11c48698-c6fd-5725-a4b0-1737e6fdc309" "question-dbe4c4ed-7bf7-5234-8564-800989eb5aa4"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064147 :question/problem "Consider the function $y = \dfrac{(x+3)^3}{(x+5)^6}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
y' = -\dfrac{g(x)(x+3)^2}{(x+5)^7}.
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y =  \dfrac{(x+3)^3}{(x+5)^6}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{(x+3)^{3}}{(x+5)^{6}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+3)^{3})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+5)^{6}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)-6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+5)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)-6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+5)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =3\cdot \frac{1}{x+3}-6\cdot \frac{1}{x+5} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{3}{x+3}-\frac{6}{x+5}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{3}{x+3}-\frac{6}{x+5})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y =  \dfrac{(x+3)^3}{(x+5)^6}{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{(x+3)^{3}}{(x+5)^{6}}(\frac{3}{x+3}-\frac{6}{x+5}) \\  & =\frac{(x+3)^{3}}{(x+5)^{6}}(\frac{3(x+5)-6(x+3)}{(x+3)(x+5)}) \\  & =\frac{(x+3)^{3}}{(x+5)^{6}}(\frac{-3x-3}{(x+3)(x+5)}) \\  & =-\frac{3(x+1)(x+3)^{2}}{(x+5)^{7}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x) = \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{3(x+1)}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064311 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-254041d3-aef5-5074-80f4-67b8b1344bc0" "question-06abf62c-6dfa-52f6-818c-3858ac967b34" "question-76085196-6a2f-5c76-90cb-5c742aa98a2b" "question-19b1b664-4a0c-5ebc-8d57-f886d4c9f0c2" "question-bc8a78e5-ffc8-5ad6-abfc-11fb82c73f1a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064148 :question/problem "Consider the function $y = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{x^2}{x^5+ 1}}.$  The derivative of this function is given by

$$
y' =  \dfrac{g(x)}{3\sqrt[3]{x(x^5+1)^4}}.
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{5}+1}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}}{\sqrt[3]{{x}^{5}+1}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2/3}}{({x}^{5}+1)^{1/3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2/3}}{({x}^{5}+1)^{1/3}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2/3})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{5}+1)^{1/3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{5}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{5}+1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{5}+1}\cdot (5{x}^{4}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{2}{x}-\frac{5{x}^{4}}{{x}^{5}+1})\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{1}{3}(\frac{2}{x}-\frac{5{x}^{4}}{{x}^{5}+1}))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y =  \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{x^2}{x^5+ 1}}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{5}+1}}(\frac{2}{x}-\frac{5{x}^{4}}{{x}^{5}+1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{5}+1}}(\frac{2({x}^{5}+1)-5{x}^{5}}{x({x}^{5}+1)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{5}+1}}(\frac{-3{x}^{5}+2}{x({x}^{5}+1)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{5}+1}}(\frac{-3{x}^{5}+2}{\sqrt[3]{{x}^{3}({x}^{5}+1)^{3}}}) \\  & =\frac{-3{x}^{5}+2}{3\sqrt[3]{x({x}^{5}+1)^{4}}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x) = \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{-3x^5+2}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-1d911ae7-875c-567e-a470-7c373f982af8" :question/id #uuid "1d911ae7-875c-567e-a470-7c373f982af8" :question/math-academy-id "q-343542" :question/problem "Given that $y=({x}^{2}+1)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{x},$ find ${y}^{′}.$

${y}^{′}=(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{x}($
{{field-1}}$\,+\,2x+x({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=({x}^{2}+1)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{x}.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+1)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot (2x)+(x)^{′}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=({x}^{2}+1)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =({x}^{2}+1)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{x}(\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x\operatorname{cot}⁡x) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{x}(2x+({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+x({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cot}⁡x) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{x}(({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+2x+x({x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2f1e7c1d-bc39-5ec5-a66f-51aa65b8b878"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-2f1e7c1d-bc39-5ec5-a66f-51aa65b8b878" :answer-field/id #uuid "2f1e7c1d-bc39-5ec5-a66f-51aa65b8b878" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-237677c3-f4bf-5920-adb2-829ac28f98fd" :answer-field/choices ["answer-237677c3-f4bf-5920-adb2-829ac28f98fd"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-237677c3-f4bf-5920-adb2-829ac28f98fd" :answer/id #uuid "237677c3-f4bf-5920-adb2-829ac28f98fd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(x^2+1)\ln(\sin x)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-62910e77-69f8-56ea-ac31-ee2dbfe3c8ff" :question/id #uuid "62910e77-69f8-56ea-ac31-ee2dbfe3c8ff" :question/math-academy-id "q-312655" :question/problem "Given that $y=({x}^{3}-2x){e}^{{x}^{4}+5x},$ find ${y}^{′}.$

$$
y=({x}^{3}-2x){e}^{{x}^{4}+5x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{3}-2x){e}^{{x}^{4}+5x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}-2x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{x}^{4}+5x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}-2x)+{x}^{4}+5x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}-2x)+{x}^{4}+5x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{3{x}^{2}-2}{{x}^{3}-2x}+4{x}^{3}+5 \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{3{x}^{2}-2}{{x}^{3}-2x}+4{x}^{3}+5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{3{x}^{2}-2}{{x}^{3}-2x}+4{x}^{3}+5)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=({x}^{3}-2x){e}^{{x}^{4}+5x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =({x}^{3}-2x){e}^{{x}^{4}+5x}(\frac{3{x}^{2}-2}{{x}^{3}-2x}+4{x}^{3}+5) \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{4}+5x}[3{x}^{2}-2+(4{x}^{3}+5)({x}^{3}-2x)] \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{4}+5x}(4{x}^{6}-8{x}^{4}+5{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-10x-2)\end{aligned}

:question/math-academy-id "q-312658" :question/problem "Given that $y={x}^{x}\operatorname{tan}⁡x,$ find ${y}^{′}.$

${y}^{′}={x}^{x}($
{{field-1}}$+\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)+{sec}^{2}⁡(x))$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y={x}^{x}\operatorname{tan}⁡x.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{x}\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{x})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(x)^{′}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{′}+{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)]}^{′} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={x}^{x}\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{x}\operatorname{tan}⁡x(\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}) \\  & ={x}^{x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & ={x}^{x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}) \\  & ={x}^{x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}) \\  & ={x}^{x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x+{sec}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6bed9cfc-3a69-5d51-ba57-741bfaabbf0a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-6bed9cfc-3a69-5d51-ba57-741bfaabbf0a" :answer-field/id #uuid "6bed9cfc-3a69-5d51-ba57-741bfaabbf0a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-0f4721e6-a280-5e36-9c3e-3d0197e080fb" :answer-field/choices ["answer-0f4721e6-a280-5e36-9c3e-3d0197e080fb"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0f4721e6-a280-5e36-9c3e-3d0197e080fb" :answer/id #uuid "0f4721e6-a280-5e36-9c3e-3d0197e080fb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\tan(x)\ln(x)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-174736f7-0588-55bb-bfa7-155dc6d18a73" :question/id #uuid "174736f7-0588-55bb-bfa7-155dc6d18a73" :question/math-academy-id "q-138800" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=({x}^{4}+1){3}^{x+4}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}={3}^{x+4}\cdot (a{x}^{4}+b{x}^{3}+c).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=({x}^{4}+1){3}^{x+4}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{4}+1){3}^{x+4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+1)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x+4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+1)+(x+4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+1)+(x+4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{4}+1}\cdot 4{x}^{3}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=({x}^{4}+1){3}^{x+4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =({x}^{4}+1){3}^{x+4}(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)) \\  & ={3}^{x+4}(4{x}^{3}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)({x}^{4}+1)) \\  & ={3}^{x+4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3){x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+4+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)=4+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-dde27e2d-4a7c-5959-b482-0d3df3d32fab"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-dde27e2d-4a7c-5959-b482-0d3df3d32fab" :answer-field/id #uuid "dde27e2d-4a7c-5959-b482-0d3df3d32fab" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-4cefdade-e796-5084-a7a3-e6383c60ef43" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4cefdade-e796-5084-a7a3-e6383c60ef43" "answer-9e897ff6-74eb-563e-ad6f-9b136723fdd4" "answer-c5bd5208-208d-5b00-a104-e894b45eded1" "answer-629e95fd-c8c0-5fb3-a0d4-61fa413fa7de" "answer-698dcec7-e3e1-5e7e-94be-301f09412429"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4cefdade-e796-5084-a7a3-e6383c60ef43" :answer/id #uuid "4cefdade-e796-5084-a7a3-e6383c60ef43" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9e897ff6-74eb-563e-ad6f-9b136723fdd4" :answer/id #uuid "9e897ff6-74eb-563e-ad6f-9b136723fdd4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c5bd5208-208d-5b00-a104-e894b45eded1" :answer/id #uuid "c5bd5208-208d-5b00-a104-e894b45eded1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-629e95fd-c8c0-5fb3-a0d4-61fa413fa7de" :answer/id #uuid "629e95fd-c8c0-5fb3-a0d4-61fa413fa7de" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-698dcec7-e3e1-5e7e-94be-301f09412429" :answer/id #uuid "698dcec7-e3e1-5e7e-94be-301f09412429" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-b9ab7545-6c81-5c20-9f25-5d780715f99d" :question/id #uuid "b9ab7545-6c81-5c20-9f25-5d780715f99d" :question/math-academy-id "q-343327" :question/problem "Given that $y={(2x-3)}^{7}{({x}^{3}+5)}^{4},$ find ${y}^{′}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({(2x-3)}^{7}{({x}^{3}+5)}^{4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({(2x-3)}^{7})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({({x}^{3}+5)}^{4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =7\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x-3)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}+5)\end{aligned}

:question/math-academy-id "q-338291" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\frac{(x+2)^{4}}{{({x}^{3}+2x-1)}^{3}}.$  Find the derivative of $y.$

| ${y}^{′}$ | $=$ | $(x+2)^{3}\,(-5{x}^{3}\,-$

{{field-2}}$x\,-$
{{field-3}}$)$ |

|  |  | ${({x}^{3}+2x-1)}^{4}$ |" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{(x+2)^{4}}{{({x}^{3}+2x-1)}^{3}}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{(x+2)^{4}}{{({x}^{3}+2x-1)}^{3}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+2)^{4})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({({x}^{3}+2x-1)}^{3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}+2x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2))-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}+2x-1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =4\cdot \frac{1}{x+2}-3\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{3}+2x-1}\cdot (3{x}^{2}+2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{4}{x+2}-\frac{3(3{x}^{2}+2)}{{x}^{3}+2x-1} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{4}{x+2}-\frac{9{x}^{2}+6}{{x}^{3}+2x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{4}{x+2}-\frac{9{x}^{2}+6}{{x}^{3}+2x-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{(x+2)^{4}}{{({x}^{3}+2x-1)}^{3}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{(x+2)^{4}}{{({x}^{3}+2x-1)}^{3}}(\frac{4}{x+2}-\frac{9{x}^{2}+6}{{x}^{3}+2x-1}) \\  & =\frac{(x+2)^{4}}{{({x}^{3}+2x-1)}^{3}}(\frac{4({x}^{3}+2x-1)-(x+2)(9{x}^{2}+6)}{(x+2)({x}^{3}+2x-1)}) \\  & =\frac{(x+2)^{4}}{{({x}^{3}+2x-1)}^{3}}(\frac{-5{x}^{3}-18{x}^{2}+2x-16}{(x+2)({x}^{3}+2x-1)}) \\  & =\frac{(x+2)^{3}(-5{x}^{3}-18{x}^{2}+2x-16)}{{({x}^{3}+2x-1)}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-274547bb-be34-5b65-bb9d-f32876fabd37" "answer-field-b03d9a12-bbbf-5ee1-a420-92022427414d" :question/math-academy-id "q-138830" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{(x+3)^{5}(x+8)^{4}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}(ax+63-8({x}^{2}+bx+c)\operatorname{cot}⁡x).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product, quotient, and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+3)^{6})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+8)^{5})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({sin}^{8}⁡x) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+8)-8\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+8)-8\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =6\cdot \frac{1}{x+3}+5\cdot \frac{1}{x+8}-8\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{6}{x+3}+\frac{5}{x+8}-8\operatorname{cot}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{6}{x+3}+\frac{5}{x+8}-8\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-138831" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\frac{(x+6)^{3}{cos}^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{7}}.$  The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=-\frac{(x+6)^{2}{cos}^{3}⁡x}{(x-1)^{8}}((ax+45)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(4{x}^{2}+bx+c)\operatorname{sin}⁡x).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{(x+6)^{3}{cos}^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{7}}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product, quotient, and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{(x+6)^{3}{cos}^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{7}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+6)^{3})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({cos}^{4}⁡x)-\operatorname{ln}⁡((x-1)^{7}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+6)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+6)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =3\cdot \frac{1}{x+6}+4\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-7\cdot \frac{1}{x-1} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{3}{x+6}-4\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{7}{x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{3}{x+6}-4\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{7}{x-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{(x+6)^{3}{cos}^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{7}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{(x+6)^{3}{cos}^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{7}}(\frac{3}{x+6}-4\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{7}{x-1}) \\  & =\frac{(x+6)^{3}{cos}^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{7}}(\frac{3(x-1)-4\operatorname{tan}⁡x(x+6)(x-1)-7(x+6)}{(x+6)(x-1)}) \\  & =\frac{(x+6)^{3}{cos}^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{7}}(\frac{-4x-45-4\operatorname{tan}⁡x({x}^{2}+5x-6)}{(x+6)(x-1)}) \\  & =-\frac{(x+6)^{2}{cos}^{4}⁡x}{(x-1)^{8}}(4x+45+4\operatorname{tan}⁡x({x}^{2}+5x-6)) \\  & =-\frac{(x+6)^{2}{cos}^{3}⁡x}{(x-1)^{8}}((4x+45)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+4\operatorname{tan}⁡x({x}^{2}+5x-6)\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =-\frac{(x+6)^{2}{cos}^{3}⁡x}{(x-1)^{8}}((4x+45)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x(4{x}^{2}+20x-24))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=4+20+(-24)=0.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c3dff71e-7253-5db5-a8db-526f8787e942"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c3dff71e-7253-5db5-a8db-526f8787e942" :answer-field/id #uuid "c3dff71e-7253-5db5-a8db-526f8787e942" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-d2bacdde-7997-50ac-944f-7a50e4a49e86" :answer-field/choices ["answer-deac3608-20ae-52c0-97b0-276c7fcb4d55" "answer-3e37cd6e-52b0-57de-acb7-d9a7a4ef0fe1" "answer-d2bacdde-7997-50ac-944f-7a50e4a49e86" "answer-6c234f23-48fe-556c-a0b1-24c477bfbdfa" "answer-39eac370-b597-5b13-a139-ed248af8a490"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-deac3608-20ae-52c0-97b0-276c7fcb4d55" :answer/id #uuid "deac3608-20ae-52c0-97b0-276c7fcb4d55" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3e37cd6e-52b0-57de-acb7-d9a7a4ef0fe1" :answer/id #uuid "3e37cd6e-52b0-57de-acb7-d9a7a4ef0fe1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d2bacdde-7997-50ac-944f-7a50e4a49e86" :answer/id #uuid "d2bacdde-7997-50ac-944f-7a50e4a49e86" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6c234f23-48fe-556c-a0b1-24c477bfbdfa" :answer/id #uuid "6c234f23-48fe-556c-a0b1-24c477bfbdfa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-39eac370-b597-5b13-a139-ed248af8a490" :answer/id #uuid "39eac370-b597-5b13-a139-ed248af8a490" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-dbe4c4ed-7bf7-5234-8564-800989eb5aa4" :question/id #uuid "dbe4c4ed-7bf7-5234-8564-800989eb5aa4" :question/math-academy-id "q-138839" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}-1}}{{e}^{2-4x}}((x+2)^{2}+g(x)).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+1)^{{x}^{2}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2-4x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-(2-4x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-2+4x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x+1}+4 \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x+1}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x+1}+4)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x+1}+4) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(\frac{2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}+4(x+1)}{x+1}) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}-1}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}+4(x+1)) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}-1}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}+4x+4) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}-1}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+(x+2)^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x)=2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-63b209a8-1c66-5330-a9ec-0e55e08cba8c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-254041d3-aef5-5074-80f4-67b8b1344bc0" :question/id #uuid "254041d3-aef5-5074-80f4-67b8b1344bc0" :question/math-academy-id "q-312672" :question/problem "Given that $$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{\frac{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}}{\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{1/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{1/2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)-\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{1/2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}\cdot (4{x}^{3}+4x)-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{4{x}^{3}+4x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{2} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{y}{2}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{\frac{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt{\frac{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{|{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8|}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8>0\text{ }∀x\in R$, so $|{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8|={x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8$ and we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}[\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}\cdot ({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)+\operatorname{tan}⁡x({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}(8{x}^{3}+8x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8))\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b1cca9dd-6ad8-57a8-a947-88e8f34aa52d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b1cca9dd-6ad8-57a8-a947-88e8f34aa52d" :answer-field/id #uuid "b1cca9dd-6ad8-57a8-a947-88e8f34aa52d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-419792fe-6389-5363-a771-125381c66945" :answer-field/choices ["answer-419792fe-6389-5363-a771-125381c66945"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-419792fe-6389-5363-a771-125381c66945" :answer/id #uuid "419792fe-6389-5363-a771-125381c66945" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8x^3+8x" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-06abf62c-6dfa-52f6-818c-3858ac967b34" :question/id #uuid "06abf62c-6dfa-52f6-818c-3858ac967b34" :question/math-academy-id "q-138850" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.$  The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{({x}^{2}+2x)^{5}}{3\sqrt[3]{{sin}^{2}⁡x}}((ax+36)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(b{x}^{2}+cx)\operatorname{cos}⁡x)
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{1/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{1/3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+2x)^{6})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{1/3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2x)+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2x)+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =6\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+2x}\cdot (2x+2)+\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{12(x+1)}{{x}^{2}+2x}+\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{12(x+1)}{{x}^{2}+2x}+\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(\frac{12(x+1)}{{x}^{2}+2x}+\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{3}) \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(\frac{12(x+1)}{{x}^{2}+2x}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡x}) \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(\frac{36(x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+({x}^{2}+2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{3({x}^{2}+2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡x}) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+2x)^{5}}{3\sqrt[3]{{sin}^{2}⁡x}}((36x+36)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(1{x}^{2}+2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=36+1+2=39.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c2b45ba0-9d41-52b1-8d31-cba0ed77bf02"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c2b45ba0-9d41-52b1-8d31-cba0ed77bf02" :answer-field/id #uuid "c2b45ba0-9d41-52b1-8d31-cba0ed77bf02" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-27b15c20-ae96-5510-bdf6-238327aebb07" :answer-field/choices ["answer-cfa37242-7820-582d-b32a-092b97e43ab6" "answer-9fa83dc4-ef7c-5fb9-9ca5-7ad2f609a832" "answer-f9347296-ee2c-5eec-91b9-fff04cdeed07" "answer-9420b75f-9ddc-56f2-8501-2ed81e404fc6" "answer-27b15c20-ae96-5510-bdf6-238327aebb07"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cfa37242-7820-582d-b32a-092b97e43ab6" :answer/id #uuid "cfa37242-7820-582d-b32a-092b97e43ab6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "33" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9fa83dc4-ef7c-5fb9-9ca5-7ad2f609a832" :answer/id #uuid "9fa83dc4-ef7c-5fb9-9ca5-7ad2f609a832" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "34" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f9347296-ee2c-5eec-91b9-fff04cdeed07" :answer/id #uuid "f9347296-ee2c-5eec-91b9-fff04cdeed07" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "37" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9420b75f-9ddc-56f2-8501-2ed81e404fc6" :answer/id #uuid "9420b75f-9ddc-56f2-8501-2ed81e404fc6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "38" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-27b15c20-ae96-5510-bdf6-238327aebb07" :answer/id #uuid "27b15c20-ae96-5510-bdf6-238327aebb07" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "39" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-76085196-6a2f-5c76-90cb-5c742aa98a2b" :question/id #uuid "76085196-6a2f-5c76-90cb-5c742aa98a2b" :question/math-academy-id "q-138849" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}(x-3)^{3}(a{x}^{2}+bx+c).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}} \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}}\cdot \sqrt{(x-3)^{8}} \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}(x-3)^{8/2} \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}(x-3)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}(x-3)^{4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((x-3)^{4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-3)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot 2x+4\cdot \frac{1}{x-3} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{3x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{4}{x-3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{3x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{4}{x-3})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}(\frac{3x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{4}{x-3}) \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}(\frac{3x(x-3)+4({x}^{2}+1)}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-3)}) \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}(\frac{7{x}^{2}-9x+4}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-3)}) \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}(x-3)^{4}(\frac{7{x}^{2}-9x+4}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-3)}) \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{1/2}(x-3)^{3}(7{x}^{2}-9x+4) \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}(x-3)^{3}(7{x}^{2}-9x+4)\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=7+(-9)+4=2.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1d436c14-aa02-5c1c-8f96-e30ae5edad2a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-1d436c14-aa02-5c1c-8f96-e30ae5edad2a" :answer-field/id #uuid "1d436c14-aa02-5c1c-8f96-e30ae5edad2a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-ebacda43-d38a-518b-8124-0083b7f84186" :answer-field/choices ["answer-04c28e5d-0de9-502d-81aa-7351f4920069" "answer-93851dca-79be-57a5-b496-18ef7187487f" "answer-b193db5a-f715-5820-8744-ed3301ee43c4" "answer-ebacda43-d38a-518b-8124-0083b7f84186" "answer-90c27865-1c0b-519b-81bb-de523a0ce9d7"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-04c28e5d-0de9-502d-81aa-7351f4920069" :answer/id #uuid "04c28e5d-0de9-502d-81aa-7351f4920069" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-93851dca-79be-57a5-b496-18ef7187487f" :answer/id #uuid "93851dca-79be-57a5-b496-18ef7187487f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "14" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b193db5a-f715-5820-8744-ed3301ee43c4" :answer/id #uuid "b193db5a-f715-5820-8744-ed3301ee43c4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "18" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ebacda43-d38a-518b-8124-0083b7f84186" :answer/id #uuid "ebacda43-d38a-518b-8124-0083b7f84186" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-90c27865-1c0b-519b-81bb-de523a0ce9d7" :answer/id #uuid "90c27865-1c0b-519b-81bb-de523a0ce9d7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-19b1b664-4a0c-5ebc-8d57-f886d4c9f0c2" :question/id #uuid "19b1b664-4a0c-5ebc-8d57-f886d4c9f0c2" :question/math-academy-id "q-343952" :question/problem "Given that $y=\sqrt[4]{\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{(2{x}^{2}+1)^{8}}},$ find ${y}^{′}.$

| ${y}^{′}=$ | $-$ | $x($
{{field-1}}$)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | $2(2{x}^{2}+1)^{3}\sqrt[4]{({x}^{2}+4)^{3}}$ |" :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[4]{\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{(2{x}^{2}+1)^{8}}} \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{(2{x}^{2}+1)^{8}}]}^{1/4} \\  & =({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4}(2{x}^{2}+1)^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4}(2{x}^{2}+1)^{-2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((2{x}^{2}+1)^{-2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{2}+1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\cdot (2x)-2\cdot \frac{1}{2{x}^{2}+1}\cdot (4x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{x}{2({x}^{2}+4)}-\frac{8x}{2{x}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}-\frac{16x}{2{x}^{2}+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{y}{2}(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}-\frac{16x}{2{x}^{2}+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt[4]{\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{(2{x}^{2}+1)^{8}}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt[4]{\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{(2{x}^{2}+1)^{8}}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}-\frac{16x}{2{x}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4}}{2(2{x}^{2}+1)^{2}}(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}-\frac{16x}{2{x}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4}}{2(2{x}^{2}+1)^{2}}(\frac{x(2{x}^{2}+1)-16x({x}^{2}+4)}{({x}^{2}+4)(2{x}^{2}+1)}) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4}}{2(2{x}^{2}+1)^{2}}(\frac{-14{x}^{3}-63x}{({x}^{2}+4)(2{x}^{2}+1)}) \\  & =-\frac{x(14{x}^{2}+63)}{2(2{x}^{2}+1)^{3}\sqrt[4]{({x}^{2}+4)^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-61e10619-0457-5f47-8c3c-d968af092244"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-61e10619-0457-5f47-8c3c-d968af092244" :answer-field/id #uuid "61e10619-0457-5f47-8c3c-d968af092244" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-1424a6ad-ac38-52fa-bea7-f95d3db15e1e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1424a6ad-ac38-52fa-bea7-f95d3db15e1e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1424a6ad-ac38-52fa-bea7-f95d3db15e1e" :answer/id #uuid "1424a6ad-ac38-52fa-bea7-f95d3db15e1e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "14x^2+63" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-bc8a78e5-ffc8-5ad6-abfc-11fb82c73f1a" :question/id #uuid "bc8a78e5-ffc8-5ad6-abfc-11fb82c73f1a" :question/math-academy-id "q-138865" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{a{x}^{5}+3{x}^{4}+b{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+c}{({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{3/2}\sqrt{{x}^{4}+2x}}.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{x}^{4}+2x}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+2x+2}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{4}+2x)^{1/2}}{({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{1/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{({x}^{4}+2x)^{1/2}}{({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{1/2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{4}+2x)^{1/2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{1/2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2x+2)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2x+2)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{4}+2x}\cdot (4{x}^{3}+2)-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}\cdot (2x+2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{2{x}^{3}+1}{{x}^{4}+2x}-\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{2{x}^{3}+1}{{x}^{4}+2x}-\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+2x+2})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}(\frac{2{x}^{3}+1}{{x}^{4}+2x}-\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}) \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}(\frac{(2{x}^{3}+1)({x}^{2}+2x+2)-(x+1)({x}^{4}+2x)}{({x}^{4}+2x)({x}^{2}+2x+2)}) \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}(\frac{2{x}^{5}+4{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+2x+2-({x}^{5}+{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+2x)}{({x}^{4}+2x)({x}^{2}+2x+2)}) \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}(\frac{{x}^{5}+3{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+2}{({x}^{4}+2x)({x}^{2}+2x+2)}) \\  & =\frac{1{x}^{5}+3{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+2}{({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{3/2}\sqrt{{x}^{4}+2x}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=1+4+2=7.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-de6a18ff-6676-56f5-b05e-7d4da313f1e4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-de6a18ff-6676-56f5-b05e-7d4da313f1e4" :answer-field/id #uuid "de6a18ff-6676-56f5-b05e-7d4da313f1e4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-d0164b4c-0fc5-5386-8a13-5df40b0b0015" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1ab36fdc-7bd5-5430-8835-a0815a440065" "answer-6d88a707-e10c-5afc-bea5-52cb9dd63b8c" "answer-9515e64c-16bf-58d0-b027-ae01ea34515a" "answer-7e987b10-51ae-5db1-b678-922798639d7e" "answer-d0164b4c-0fc5-5386-8a13-5df40b0b0015"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1ab36fdc-7bd5-5430-8835-a0815a440065" :answer/id #uuid "1ab36fdc-7bd5-5430-8835-a0815a440065" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6d88a707-e10c-5afc-bea5-52cb9dd63b8c" :answer/id #uuid "6d88a707-e10c-5afc-bea5-52cb9dd63b8c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9515e64c-16bf-58d0-b027-ae01ea34515a" :answer/id #uuid "9515e64c-16bf-58d0-b027-ae01ea34515a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7e987b10-51ae-5db1-b678-922798639d7e" :answer/id #uuid "7e987b10-51ae-5db1-b678-922798639d7e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d0164b4c-0fc5-5386-8a13-5df40b0b0015" :answer/id #uuid "d0164b4c-0fc5-5386-8a13-5df40b0b0015" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186065396 :tutorial/content "When a function $y=y(x)$ contains complex products, quotients, or radicals, we can use logarithmic differentiation to find the derivative $y'(x).$ 

For example, consider the following function: 

$$
y = x^2 \cdot 2^x
$$

 

Our goal is to find $y'(x).$ To do this, we will use the product rule for logarithms, namely

$$
\ln(a b)= \ln a + \ln b.
$$

 

We differentiate our function by following four steps.

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the product and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Next, we differentiate both sides of our equation using implicit differentiation:

$$

This gives

$$
-1+\frac{8}{5}=-\frac{5}{5}+\frac{8}{5}=\frac{-5+8}{5}.
$$

To compute the numerator, we can use either Method 1 or Method 2, shown below.

**Method 1 - Picturing a Number Line**

To add $8$ to $-5,$ we start at $-5$ on a number line and move $8$ spaces to the right.

![](images/0b/0b6274b1cb65e330c81602212fe081835eb86c1c1c8e3a6eee278fbfd2614776.png)

So, $-5+8=3.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{-5+8}{5}=\frac{3}{5}.
$$

**Method 2 - Subtraction in Reverse**

We can swap the order of the numbers in the numerator, and we get

$$
\frac{-5+8}{5}=\frac{8-5}{5}=\frac{3}{5}.
$$

So, we conclude that $-1+\frac{8}{5}=\frac{3}{5}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-246cfafb-6189-5729-9be6-ca9bbaab24e4"] :db/ensure "$(-5.5)^{2}=$" :question/worked-solution "We need to calculate the product of $-5.5$ with itself:

$$
(-5.5)^{2}=(-5.5)\cdot (-5.5)=(5.5)\cdot (5.5)
$$

First, we ignore the decimal points and multiply as if both numbers were whole numbers:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} &  &  & \,\,\,\,\begin{aligned}\boxed{2} \\ \boxed{2}\end{aligned}\,\,\,\, &  \\  &  &  & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,\times \,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, \\  &  & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,7\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,+\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,7\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, \\  & \,\,\,\,3\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\,\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $55\times 55=3\,025.$

We now count the total number of decimal places in the two factors.

There is $1$ decimal place in the first factor ($5.5$) and $1$ decimal place in the second factor ($5.5$), so their product will have $1+1=2$ decimal places.

We take our value of $3\,025$ and insert a decimal point to make a number with $2$ decimal places:

$$
30\,\overset{↓}{.}\,\,\,{{25}_{⏟}}_{2\text{ digits}}
$$

Therefore, ${5.5}^{2}=30.25.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c64d54dd-1bd9-5b4c-bf85-d147344d6818"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
(-15)^{2}=(-15)\cdot (-15)=15\cdot 15
$$

Next, we calculate $15\cdot 15:$

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} &  &  & \,\,\,\,\begin{aligned}\boxed{} \\ \boxed{2}\end{aligned}\,\,\,\, &  \\  &  &  & \,\,\,\,1\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,\times \,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,1\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, \\  &  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,7\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,+\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,1\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\,\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$

A hot air balloon is inflated at the rate of $12\,{\text{in}}^{3}\text{/s}.$ How fast is the radius, $r$, changing at the moment when $r=2\,\text{in}?$" :question/worked-solution "Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=12\,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=2\,\text{in}.$

To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=12$ and $r=2,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi (2)^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 16\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{4\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of the balloon is decreasing at a rate of $\frac{3}{4\pi }\,\text{in}/\text{s}$ when the radius is $2\,\text{in}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy At a particular moment, the rate of increase in the volume of the balloon is numerically equal to nine-halfs the rate of increase in its surface area. What is the radius of the balloon at that moment?" :question/worked-solution "Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon, $V$ the volume, and $A$ its surface area. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the volume $V$ and the surface area $A$ of the sphere. Since $A=4\pi {r}^{2}$ and $V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3},$ the relationship between $V$ and $A$ is

$$
V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3}=\frac{4\pi }{3}{(\frac{A}{4\pi })}^{3/2}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{3(4\pi )^{1/2}}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}A}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }} \\ {A}^{1/2} & =18\sqrt{\pi } \\ A & ={(18\sqrt{\pi })}^{2} \\ A & =324\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $A=4\pi {r}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4\pi {r}^{2} & =324\pi  \\ {r}^{2} & =81 \\ r & =9.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-893ce6e9-d2a5-5687-890a-43b20d335c93"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-893ce6e9-d2a5-5687-890a-43b20d335c93" :answer-field/id #uuid "893ce6e9-d2a5-5687-890a-43b20d335c93" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-a3ab0c31-9934-5df4-8de8-4658ed227b1a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5ad7d797-78b2-528c-9d9b-806dc635caa2" "answer-8c834b34-6910-5d98-ab6c-76660ea17f16" "answer-03e5c2fc-62c3-5cff-8c3f-12578ac7eec2" "answer-4bd9e9ba-35f5-5dc8-b23d-1b83df5ca67c" "answer-a3ab0c31-9934-5df4-8de8-4658ed227b1a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5ad7d797-78b2-528c-9d9b-806dc635caa2" :answer/id #uuid "5ad7d797-78b2-528c-9d9b-806dc635caa2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1.5\,\text{in}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8c834b34-6910-5d98-ab6c-76660ea17f16" :answer/id #uuid "8c834b34-6910-5d98-ab6c-76660ea17f16" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12.5\,\text{in}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-03e5c2fc-62c3-5cff-8c3f-12578ac7eec2" :answer/id #uuid "03e5c2fc-62c3-5cff-8c3f-12578ac7eec2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2.5\,\text{in}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4bd9e9ba-35f5-5dc8-b23d-1b83df5ca67c" :answer/id #uuid "4bd9e9ba-35f5-5dc8-b23d-1b83df5ca67c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4.5\,\text{in}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a3ab0c31-9934-5df4-8de8-4658ed227b1a" :answer/id #uuid "a3ab0c31-9934-5df4-8de8-4658ed227b1a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9\,\text{in}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-37194e35-397f-5f0f-b8ce-0e1f1331cb3b" :question/id #uuid "37194e35-397f-5f0f-b8ce-0e1f1331cb3b" :question/math-academy-id "q-344726" :question/problem "![](images/1c/1c16496b13f9ad9fc995cc59dedf1777f25e394ca61dd2ea493d8bd8f69c5e14.png)

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠A+m∠B+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠B+2m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠B+2\cdot {80}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠B+{160}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠B & ={20}^{∘}\end{aligned}

*Hint: Use the fact that ${x}^{2}-2x+1$ is a perfect square.*" :question/worked-solution "Using the hint, we have

$$
{x}^{2}-2x+1=(x-1)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-8x & =5 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2x) & =5 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2\cdot 1x) & =5 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2\cdot 1x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) & =5 \\ 4[(x-1)^{2}-{1}^{2}] & =5 \\ 4[(x-1)^{2}-1] & =5 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-4 & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by adding $4$ to both sides and then dividing by $4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-1)^{2}-4 & =5 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-4+4 & =5+4 \\ 4(x-1)^{2} & =9 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =\frac{9}{4} \\ \sqrt{(x-1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}} \\ |x-1| & =\frac{3}{2} \\ x-1 & =\pm \frac{3}{2} \\ x & =1\pm \frac{3}{2} \\ x & =-\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e38d1eab-b846-57b1-8eca-3e79f6301a02"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

Now we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+6x-10 & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x & =10 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x & =10 \\ 4({x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x) & =10 \\ 4[{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{4}x+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}] & =10 \\ 4[{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{16}] & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{9}{16} & =10 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4} & =10 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =10+\frac{9}{4} \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{49}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{3}{4}.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{49}{4} \\ {(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{49}{16} \\ \sqrt{{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{49}{16}} \\ |x+\frac{3}{4}| & =\frac{7}{4} \\ x+\frac{3}{4} & =\pm \frac{7}{4} \\ x & =-\frac{3}{4}\pm \frac{7}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{3}{4}-\frac{7}{4}=-\frac{10}{4}=-\frac{5}{2} \\ x & =-\frac{3}{4}+\frac{7}{4}=1\end{aligned}
$$
