At a particular moment, the rate of increase in the volume of the balloon is numerically equal to nine-halfs the rate of increase in its surface area. What is the radius of the balloon at that moment?" :question/worked-solution "Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon, $V$ the volume, and $A$ its surface area. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the volume $V$ and the surface area $A$ of the sphere. Since $A=4\pi {r}^{2}$ and $V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3},$ the relationship between $V$ and $A$ is

$$
V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3}=\frac{4\pi }{3}{(\frac{A}{4\pi })}^{3/2}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{3(4\pi )^{1/2}}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}A}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }} \\ {A}^{1/2} & =18\sqrt{\pi } \\ A & ={(18\sqrt{\pi })}^{2} \\ A & =324\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $A=4\pi {r}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4\pi {r}^{2} & =324\pi  \\ {r}^{2} & =81 \\ r & =9.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-893ce6e9-d2a5-5687-890a-43b20d335c93"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-893ce6e9-d2a5-5687-890a-43b20d335c93" :answer-field/id #uuid "893ce6e9-d2a5-5687-890a-43b20d335c93" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-a3ab0c31-9934-5df4-8de8-4658ed227b1a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5ad7d797-78b2-528c-9d9b-806dc635caa2" "answer-8c834b34-6910-5d98-ab6c-76660ea17f16" "answer-03e5c2fc-62c3-5cff-8c3f-12578ac7eec2" "answer-4bd9e9ba-35f5-5dc8-b23d-1b83df5ca67c" "answer-a3ab0c31-9934-5df4-8de8-4658ed227b1a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5ad7d797-78b2-528c-9d9b-806dc635caa2" :answer/id #uuid "5ad7d797-78b2-528c-9d9b-806dc635caa2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1.5\,\text{in}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8c834b34-6910-5d98-ab6c-76660ea17f16" :answer/id #uuid "8c834b34-6910-5d98-ab6c-76660ea17f16" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12.5\,\text{in}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-03e5c2fc-62c3-5cff-8c3f-12578ac7eec2" :answer/id #uuid "03e5c2fc-62c3-5cff-8c3f-12578ac7eec2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2.5\,\text{in}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4bd9e9ba-35f5-5dc8-b23d-1b83df5ca67c" :answer/id #uuid "4bd9e9ba-35f5-5dc8-b23d-1b83df5ca67c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4.5\,\text{in}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a3ab0c31-9934-5df4-8de8-4658ed227b1a" :answer/id #uuid "a3ab0c31-9934-5df4-8de8-4658ed227b1a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9\,\text{in}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-37194e35-397f-5f0f-b8ce-0e1f1331cb3b" :question/id #uuid "37194e35-397f-5f0f-b8ce-0e1f1331cb3b" :question/math-academy-id "q-344726" :question/problem "![](images/1c/1c16496b13f9ad9fc995cc59dedf1777f25e394ca61dd2ea493d8bd8f69c5e14.png)

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠A+m∠B+m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠B+2m∠C & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠B+2\cdot {80}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠B+{160}^{∘} & ={180}^{∘} \\ m∠B & ={20}^{∘}\end{aligned}

*Hint: Use the fact that ${x}^{2}-2x+1$ is a perfect square.*" :question/worked-solution "Using the hint, we have

$$
{x}^{2}-2x+1=(x-1)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-8x & =5 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2x) & =5 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2\cdot 1x) & =5 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2\cdot 1x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) & =5 \\ 4[(x-1)^{2}-{1}^{2}] & =5 \\ 4[(x-1)^{2}-1] & =5 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-4 & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by adding $4$ to both sides and then dividing by $4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-1)^{2}-4 & =5 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-4+4 & =5+4 \\ 4(x-1)^{2} & =9 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =\frac{9}{4} \\ \sqrt{(x-1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}} \\ |x-1| & =\frac{3}{2} \\ x-1 & =\pm \frac{3}{2} \\ x & =1\pm \frac{3}{2} \\ x & =-\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e38d1eab-b846-57b1-8eca-3e79f6301a02"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

Now we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+6x-10 & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x & =10 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x & =10 \\ 4({x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x) & =10 \\ 4[{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{4}x+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}] & =10 \\ 4[{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{16}] & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{9}{16} & =10 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4} & =10 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =10+\frac{9}{4} \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{49}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{3}{4}.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{49}{4} \\ {(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{49}{16} \\ \sqrt{{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{49}{16}} \\ |x+\frac{3}{4}| & =\frac{7}{4} \\ x+\frac{3}{4} & =\pm \frac{7}{4} \\ x & =-\frac{3}{4}\pm \frac{7}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{3}{4}-\frac{7}{4}=-\frac{10}{4}=-\frac{5}{2} \\ x & =-\frac{3}{4}+\frac{7}{4}=1\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}  liters of water in the tank at $5\,\text{p.m}.$" :question/worked-solution "Water is flowing into the tank at a rate of $6t+10$ liters per hour and is draining at a rate of $8$ liters per hour. Therefore, the **rate of change** in the amount of water (call it $R(t)$) is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(t) & =r(t)-8 \\  & =6t+10-8 \\  & =6t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the **total amount of water** after $t$ hours (call it $T(t)$), we apply the second fundamental theorem of calculus:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =T(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}R(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =200+{\int }_{0}^{t}(6x+2)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To ensure that $T$ is a function of $t$ only, we use a different variable ($x$) for the integration. 

To find out the amount of water after $4$ hours ($5\,\text{p.m}$), we substitute $t=4$ into the above and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(4) & =200+{\int }_{0}^{4}(6x+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =200+(3{x}^{2}+2x){|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =200+[(3\cdot 16+8)-0] \\  & =200+56 \\  & =256\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there will be $256$ liters of water in the tank at $5\,\text{p.m}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bdb50e03-36f7-5d1f-9178-33250a489690"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-bdb50e03-36f7-5d1f-9178-33250a489690" :answer-field/id #uuid "bdb50e03-36f7-5d1f-9178-33250a489690" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-e6f34e98-745c-508e-9aac-c7930cd0847b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e6f34e98-745c-508e-9aac-c7930cd0847b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e6f34e98-745c-508e-9aac-c7930cd0847b" :answer/id #uuid "e6f34e98-745c-508e-9aac-c7930cd0847b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "256" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-7896667b-b339-512f-9dbb-66fd90855442" :question/id #uuid "7896667b-b339-512f-9dbb-66fd90855442" :question/math-academy-id "q-349984" :question/problem "A city is tracking the number of bikes available in a bike-share station.
They observe that bikes are returned to the station at a rate $r(t)$ given by the function

$$
r(t)=5{t}^{3}+2t,
$$

where $r(t)$ is measured in bikes per hour, and $t>0$ is the time in hours since tracking began.

If there were initially $100$ bikes at the station, find the expression that gives $B(t),$ the number of bikes at the station $t$ hours after tracking began.

$B(t)=\frac{5}{4}{t}^{4}\,+$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The number of bikes is increasing at a rate of $r(t)$ bikes per hour and is decreasing at a rate of $4$ bikes per hour. Therefore, the **rate of change** $R(t)$ of the number of bikes is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(t) & =r(t)-4 \\  & =5{t}^{3}+2t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the total number $B(t)$ of bikes after $t$ hours, we apply the second fundamental theorem of calculus:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =B(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}R(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =100+{\int }_{0}^{t}(5{x}^{3}+2x-4)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To ensure that our final function is a function of $t$ only, we use a different variable ($x$) for the integration.

We can simplify the expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =100+{\int }_{0}^{t}5{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{t}2x\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{0}^{t}4\,\text{d}x \\  & =100+{5\,\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{t}+{2\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{t}-4x{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =100+\frac{5}{4}{t}^{4}+{t}^{2}-4t \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{t}^{4}+\,{t}^{2}-4t+100\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9eaf115f-1435-52c2-b951-5e9b2f69cb63"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9eaf115f-1435-52c2-b951-5e9b2f69cb63" :answer-field/id #uuid "9eaf115f-1435-52c2-b951-5e9b2f69cb63" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-b9635b2b-705b-58e9-94bd-88166205012c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b9635b2b-705b-58e9-94bd-88166205012c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b9635b2b-705b-58e9-94bd-88166205012c" :answer/id #uuid "b9635b2b-705b-58e9-94bd-88166205012c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "t^{2}-4t+100" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-54f0409c-f2ef-5cc4-b4e4-ffc38eb896a2" :question/id #uuid "54f0409c-f2ef-5cc4-b4e4-ffc38eb896a2" :question/math-academy-id "q-349997" :question/problem "On a certain afternoon, the total number of people $N(t)$ visiting the city's zoo is given by the function

$$
N(t)=30+4{\int }_{0}^{t}(10-2x)\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time (in hours) since noon.

The maximum number of people is
{{field-1}}

{{field-2}}
hours." :question/worked-solution "To find when the number of people at the zoo is at maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}N}{\text{d}t}=0.$ First, we differentiate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}N}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(30+4{\int }_{0}^{t}(10-2x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(30)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{\int }_{0}^{t}(10-2x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{0}^{t}(10-2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4(10-2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve $\frac{\text{d}N}{\text{d}t}=0$:

$$
4(10-2t)=0\,⟹\,t=5
$$

So there are two candidates for global extrema, $t=0$ and $t=5.$ To find out how many people are in the zoo when $t=5,$ we figure out $N(5):$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(5) & =30+4{\int }_{0}^{5}(10-2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =30+4{[10x-{x}^{2}]|}_{0}^{5} \\  & =30+4[(10\cdot 5-{5}^{2})-(0)] \\  & =30+4\cdot 25 \\  & =130\end{aligned}
$$

Since $30<130$, we conclude that the maximum number of people at the zoo is $130$, and this will happen after $5$ hours." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ![](images/fa/fa23c036920e2c506c38f1e7be8a498c0a349ef145e8c444201665345bc648e4.png)

We call $\color{blue}\angle{CBE}$ the **exterior angle** of the vertex $B$.

Given a polygon's vertex, the interior and exterior angles are supplementary. So, for the vertex $B,$ we have:

$$
\underbrace{\color{YellowOrange}m\angle{ABC}}_{\large\text{Interior}} \:+\: \underbrace{\color{blue}m\angle{CBE}}_{\large\text{Exterior}} = 180^\circ
$$

We have the following theorem:

The measures of the exterior angles of any simple polygon sum to $360^\circ.$

We'll show why this theorem is true at the end of the lesson.

Let's label the exterior angles of our polygon below:

![](images/ac/acc0ac90f27a78e83b6b14651f61ddfe6a87afa56b6e51a1af57f5e74c31689f.png)

According to our theorem, these four angles sum to $360^\circ.$

$$
a+b+c+d = 360^\circ
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107163 :tutorial/content "Why do the exterior angles of a polygon always sum to $360^\circ?$

Suppose we have an $n$-sided polygon. Then, we have the following:

- There are $n$ pairs of interior-exterior angles, each pair being supplementary (i.e., their measures add to $180^\circ).$

- Therefore, the sum of the measures of *all* interior-exterior pairs equals ${\color{blue}n\cdot 180^\circ}.$

- In a previous lesson, we saw that the sum of the *interior* angles equals ${\color{red}{(n-2)\cdot 180^\circ}}.$

Therefore, to get the sum of the *exterior* angles, we subtract ${\color{red}{(n-2)\cdot 180^\circ}}$ from ${\color{blue}n\cdot 180^\circ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Sum of Exterior Angles} & =n\cdot {180}^{∘}-(n-2)\cdot {180}^{∘} \\  & =n\cdot {180}^{∘}-n\cdot {180}^{∘}+2\cdot {180}^{∘} \\  & =\cancel{n\cdot {180}^{∘}}-\cancel{n\cdot {180}^{∘}}+2\cdot {180}^{∘} \\  & =2\cdot {180}^{∘} \\  & ={360}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

This proves that the sum of the exterior angles of a (simple) polygon equals $360^\circ.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105975 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186478315 :answer-field/correct "answer-d5430906-9808-587e-9c79-133123248909" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d5430906-9808-587e-9c79-133123248909"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d5430906-9808-587e-9c79-133123248909" :answer/id #uuid "d5430906-9808-587e-9c79-133123248909" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value ">" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186084596 :answer-field/choices 17592186084597] [:db/retract 17592186084596 :answer-field/choices 17592186084598] [:db/retract 17592186084596 :answer-field/choices 17592186084599] [:db/retract 17592186084596 :answer-field/choices 17592186084600] [:db/retract 17592186084596 :answer-field/choices 17592186084601] [:db/retract 17592186084602 :answer-field/choices 17592186084603] [:db/retract 17592186084602 :answer-field/choices 17592186084604] [:db/retract 17592186084602 :answer-field/choices 17592186084605] [:db/retract 17592186084602 :answer-field/choices 17592186084606] [:db/retract 17592186084602 :answer-field/choices 17592186084607] {:db/id 17592186087835 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-38e098ba-2563-5c51-8af3-272acb29f55b"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087836 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8c404e97-7fab-5c9d-b54c-fbf58817ca24"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087838 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c693f3f3-9251-58ce-8006-d594413ed6b7" "question-48e55e9e-f8d4-5cc0-b60c-cb504ca3f4b2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-38e098ba-2563-5c51-8af3-272acb29f55b" :question/id #uuid "38e098ba-2563-5c51-8af3-272acb29f55b" :question/math-academy-id "q-277800" :question/problem "From **left to right,** the $x$-intercepts of the hyperbola $9{x}^{2}-16{y}^{2}=144$ are

First, we substitute $(-8,-2)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{4} \\ (-2) & =\frac{-8}{4} \\ -2 & =-2\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

The result is a true statement, so $(-8,-2)$ is a solution to the equation.

Next, we substitute $(4,1)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{4} \\ (1) & =\frac{4}{4} \\ 1 & =1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

The result is again a true statement, so $(4,1)$ is also a solution to the equation.

Finally, we substitute $(-4,1)$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{4} \\ (1) & =\frac{-4}{4} \\ 1 & =-1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

The result is a false statement, so $(-4,1)$ is *not* a solution to the equation.

$$
\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

To rewrite the equation of the hyperbola in standard form, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}+6x+8y & =-1 \\ {x}^{2}+6x\,-\,4{y}^{2}+8y & =-1 \\ [{x}^{2}+6x]\,-\,4[{y}^{2}-2y] & =-1 \\ [(x+3)^{2}-9]\,-\,4[(y-1)^{2}-1] & =-1 \\ (x+3)^{2}-9\,-\,4(y-1)^{2}+4 & =-1 \\ (x+3)^{2}-4(y-1)^{2} & =-1+9-4 \\ (x+3)^{2}-4(y-1)^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{(x-(-3))^{2}}{{2}^{2}}-\frac{(y-1)^{2}}{{1}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the center of the hyperbola is $(\,-3,1\,).$"] ["question-1b9ba30c-75b9-548b-bbd4-b9dfefeaa769" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] $$

$$

- On the interval $(-\infty ,1],$ we have a line with slope $2$ and $y$-intercept $1.$ So the graph is the line $y=2x+1$ that ends at $(1,3),$ including this point.

- On the interval $(1,\infty )$, we have a line with a slope of $-2$ that passes through the point $(1,0).$ We can find the equation of this line using point-slope form:

$$
y-0=-2(x-1)\,⟹\,y=2-2x
$$

So the graph is the line $y=2-2x$ that starts at $(1,0),$ excluding this point.

Therefore, the function is defined as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6a\,\, & >\,\,-12 \\ \frac{-6a}{-6}\, & <\,\,\frac{-12}{-6} \\ \frac{-6a}{-6}\, & <\,\,2\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-6a}{-6} & <2 \\ \frac{\cancel{-6}a}{\cancel{-6}} & <2 \\ a & <2\end{aligned}
$$

$$

x \gt 4

:question/problem "Represent the solution of the inequality $-\frac{a}{4}>-2$ on a number line."] ["question-5f4cf73b-e442-544c-845a-c7e6521bdf69" :question/worked-solution "The variable $a$ is being *divided* by $4.$ To isolate $a$ and remove the negative sign, we *multiply* by $-4.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{a}{4}\,\, & >\,\,-2 \\ (-4)\cdot (-\frac{a}{4})\,\, & <\,\,(-4)\cdot (-2) \\ (-4)\cdot (-\frac{a}{4})\,\, & <\,\,8\end{aligned}
$$

Since two negative numbers multiply to give a positive number, we first cancel the negatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)\cdot (-\frac{a}{4}) & <8 \\ (\cancel{-}4)\cdot (\cancel{-}\frac{a}{4}) & <8 \\ 4\cdot \frac{a}{4} & <8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $4$ from both the numerator and denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot \frac{a}{4} & <8 \\ \frac{4a}{4} & <8 \\ \frac{\cancel{4}a}{\cancel{4}} & <8 \\ a & <8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $a<8.$ The solution can be expressed on a number line, as shown below.

$$

Finally, let's swap the left and right-hand sides so that the variable is on the left-hand side. Remember, we also need to flip the inequality.

$$
x\ge -1
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+3 & \le 7 \\ -2x+3-3 & \le 7-3 \\ -2x+0 & \le 4 \\ -2x & \le 4\end{aligned}
$$

Remember, when multiplying or dividing by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x\,\, & \le \,\,4 \\ \frac{-2x}{-2}\, & \ge \,\,\frac{4}{-2} \\ \frac{\cancel{-2}x}{\cancel{-2}}\, & \ge \,\,-2 \\ x\,\, & \ge \,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\ge -2.$ The solution can be expressed on a number line, as shown below.

represent the solution of an inequality using a number line.

For example, let's express the solution of the following inequality using a number line:

$$
5x \geq 30
$$

The variable $x$ is being *multiplied* by $5.$ To isolate $x,$ we can perform the *opposite* operation, which is *dividing* by $5.$ So, we divide both sides of the inequality by $5{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}5x & \ge 30 \\ \frac{5x}{5} & \ge \frac{30}{5} \\ \frac{5x}{5} & \ge 6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can cancel a common factor of $5$ from the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5x}{5} & \ge 6 \\ \frac{\cancel{5}x}{\cancel{5}} & \ge 6 \\ x & \ge 6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x \geq 6.$ This solution can be expressed on a number line, as shown below.

find the inverse Laplace transform of $G(s),$ given that
$L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.$"] [17592186370079 :question/worked-solution "Notice that we can write $G(s)$ as 

$$
G(s)=\frac{6}{{s}^{5}}=\frac{F(s)}{s},
$$

where $F(s)=\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{F(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{3!}{{s}^{3+1}}\} \\  & ={t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$, then

$$
L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{G(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{F(s)}{s}\} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{τ}^{3}\,\text{d}τ \\  & =\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-90de09a4-cb73-52eb-bce8-60541ed9cd90" :question/id #uuid "90de09a4-cb73-52eb-bce8-60541ed9cd90"] ["question-90de09a4-cb73-52eb-bce8-60541ed9cd90" :question/math-academy-id "q-330844"] ["question-90de09a4-cb73-52eb-bce8-60541ed9cd90" :question/problem "For the function

$$

where $F(s)=\frac{120}{{s}^{6}}.$
Also, we know that

$$
L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{F(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{120}{{s}^{6}}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{5!}{{s}^{5+1}}\} \\  & ={t}^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we know that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$, then

$$
L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\}=\frac{F(s)}{s}.
$$

Using the property above in reverse, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{-1}\{G(s)\} & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{F(s)}{s}\} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}{τ}^{5}\,\text{d}τ \\  & =\frac{{t}^{6}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-90de09a4-cb73-52eb-bce8-60541ed9cd90" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-c608cf93-4730-5e85-9788-45b64178d3fb" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Suppose we wish to find $L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}$ given $L\{f(t)\}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ=A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t}={{field-1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ\}=L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & ⇒ & du={{field-3}} \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }({{field-4}}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=$ {{field-5}}, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-6}}\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e8bb9695-808d-511b-81de-dd222d55651d" :question/worked-solution "Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\} & =L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ we have $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=0$ and

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e8bb9695-808d-511b-81de-dd222d55651d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-2161928e-f74f-573a-af14-39c0404a2ddd" :answer-field/id #uuid ."] ["question-1fff8974-347e-5cb7-8b9b-0077208b27ab" :question/worked-solution "Let $A(t)$ be the anti-derivative of $f(t)$ such that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t)$ and $A(0)=0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,dτ & =A(τ)\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =A(t)-A(0) \\  & =A(t).\end{aligned}
$$

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{\int }_{0}^{t}f(τ)\,\text{d}τ\} & =L\{A(t)\}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's use integration by parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=A(t) & \,⇒\, & du={A}^{′}(t)\,dt \\ dv={e}^{-st}\,dt & ⇒ & v=-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt & =A(t)(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})\,{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}){A}^{′}(t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A(0)=0$ and $\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ we have $-\frac{1}{s}A(t){e}^{-st}{|}_{0}^{\infty }=0$ and

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}A(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt.
$$

Finally, using that ${A}^{′}(t)=f(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{A}^{′}(t)\,dt & =\frac{1}{s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt \\  & =\frac{1}{s}\cdot F(s) \\  & =\frac{F(s)}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1fff8974-347e-5cb7-8b9b-0077208b27ab" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-6aa65c38-ceb5-5eee-933c-ee1420bc034b" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-088aa711-4888-53e6-84c3-09dd07764006" :question/math-academy-id "q-89409"] ["question-088aa711-4888-53e6-84c3-09dd07764006" :question/problem "A fair spinner has three regions, red, blue, and green. Suppose the spinner is spun $21$ times. What is the variance of the number of times the spinner lands on blue?"] ["question-088aa711-4888-53e6-84c3-09dd07764006" :question/worked-solution "Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times the spinner lands on blue.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=21$ trials

- the probability of landing on blue is

$$
p=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(21,\frac{1}{3}).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the variance is given by

$$
\text{Var}[X]=np(1-p),
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the variance of the number of times the spinner lands on blue is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =np(1-p) \\  & =21\cdot \frac{1}{3}\cdot (1-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =7\cdot \frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{14}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-088aa711-4888-53e6-84c3-09dd07764006" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-2db3a67a-7d60-5de0-94bb-64450c65d4fe" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-83d9fcb6-7217-5c43-a034-d390b057ff4d" :question/math-academy-id "q-181954"] ["question-83d9fcb6-7217-5c43-a034-d390b057ff4d" :question/problem "Which of the following is a representation of the set $S=\{-2,2\}\times {N}_{0}$ in the Cartesian plane?"] ["question-83d9fcb6-7217-5c43-a034-d390b057ff4d" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=\{-2,2\}\times {N}_{0}
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is either $-2$ or $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is a natural number or zero.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in \{-2,2\},\,y\in {N}_{0}\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{-2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $-2$ and whose $y$-coordinate  is any natural number or zero.

$$
{S}_{-2}=\{(-2,y)\,:\,y\in {N}_{0}\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-2}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/44/4418001fb8fb44cc5cd35b258136ee696d35d27198549177a2f60a7297d31bb1.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $2$ and whose $y$-coordinate  is any natural number or zero.

$$
{S}_{2}=\{(2,y)\,:\,y\in {N}_{0}\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{2}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/bf/bf74df976235b72a24047e2ec27aad7d426b6ceb1fcb948bc656b77bf0635911.png)

Our Cartesian product $S$ is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={S}_{-2}\cup {S}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $\{-2,2\}\times {N}_{0}$ as the set of points in the diagram below.

- The shape $P$ is a rectangle. The sides are not all congruent, so it is not a rhombus.

- The shape $Q$ is a square. All its sides are congruent and the opposite sides are parallel, so it is a rhombus.

- The shape $R$ is a trapezoid. Since it has only one pair of parallel sides, it is not a rhombus.

- The shape $S$ is an isosceles trapezoid.  Since it has only one pair of parallel sides, it is not a rhombus.

{{field-1}}$+\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)+{sec}^{2}⁡(x))$"] ["question-61a2565a-e401-5260-aae7-f12b167eb293" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y={x}^{x}\operatorname{tan}⁡x.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{x}\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{x})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(x)^{′}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{′}+{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)]}^{′} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={x}^{x}\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{x}\operatorname{tan}⁡x(\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}) \\  & ={x}^{x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & ={x}^{x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}) \\  & ={x}^{x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}) \\  & ={x}^{x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x+{sec}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-61a2565a-e401-5260-aae7-f12b167eb293" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-6bed9cfc-3a69-5d51-ba57-741bfaabbf0a" :answer-field/id #uuid "6bed9cfc-3a69-5d51-ba57-741bfaabbf0a"] ["answer-0f4721e6-a280-5e36-9c3e-3d0197e080fb" :answer/id #uuid "0f4721e6-a280-5e36-9c3e-3d0197e080fb"] ["answer-0f4721e6-a280-5e36-9c3e-3d0197e080fb" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-0f4721e6-a280-5e36-9c3e-3d0197e080fb" :answer/value "\tan(x)\ln(x)"] ["answer-field-6bed9cfc-3a69-5d51-ba57-741bfaabbf0a" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-6bed9cfc-3a69-5d51-ba57-741bfaabbf0a" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-6bed9cfc-3a69-5d51-ba57-741bfaabbf0a" :answer-field/correct "answer-0f4721e6-a280-5e36-9c3e-3d0197e080fb"] ["answer-field-6bed9cfc-3a69-5d51-ba57-741bfaabbf0a" :answer-field/choices "answer-0f4721e6-a280-5e36-9c3e-3d0197e080fb"] ["question-61a2565a-e401-5260-aae7-f12b167eb293" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-6bed9cfc-3a69-5d51-ba57-741bfaabbf0a"] [17592186064309 :knowledge-point/questions "question-61a2565a-e401-5260-aae7-f12b167eb293"] ["question-174736f7-0588-55bb-bfa7-155dc6d18a73" :question/id #uuid "174736f7-0588-55bb-bfa7-155dc6d18a73"] ["question-174736f7-0588-55bb-bfa7-155dc6d18a73" :question/math-academy-id "q-138800"] ["question-174736f7-0588-55bb-bfa7-155dc6d18a73" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=({x}^{4}+1){3}^{x+4}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$"] ["question-174736f7-0588-55bb-bfa7-155dc6d18a73" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=({x}^{4}+1){3}^{x+4}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{4}+1){3}^{x+4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+1)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x+4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+1)+(x+4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+1)+(x+4)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{4}+1}\cdot 4{x}^{3}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=({x}^{4}+1){3}^{x+4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =({x}^{4}+1){3}^{x+4}(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}+1}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)) \\  & ={3}^{x+4}(4{x}^{3}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)({x}^{4}+1)) \\  & ={3}^{x+4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3){x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+4+\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)=4+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3).
$$"] ["question-174736f7-0588-55bb-bfa7-155dc6d18a73" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-dde27e2d-4a7c-5959-b482-0d3df3d32fab" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
y=\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product, quotient, and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+3)^{6})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+8)^{5})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({sin}^{8}⁡x) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+8)-8\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+3)+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+8)-8\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =6\cdot \frac{1}{x+3}+5\cdot \frac{1}{x+8}-8\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{6}{x+3}+\frac{5}{x+8}-8\operatorname{cot}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{6}{x+3}+\frac{5}{x+8}-8\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}(\frac{6}{x+3}+\frac{5}{x+8}-8\operatorname{cot}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}(\frac{6(x+8)+5(x+3)-8\operatorname{cot}⁡x(x+3)(x+8)}{(x+3)(x+8)}) \\  & =\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}(\frac{6x+48+5x+15-8\operatorname{cot}⁡x({x}^{2}+11x+24)}{(x+3)(x+8)}) \\  & =\frac{(x+3)^{6}(x+8)^{5}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}(\frac{11x+63-8\operatorname{cot}⁡x({x}^{2}+11x+24)}{(x+3)(x+8)}) \\  & =\frac{(x+3)^{5}(x+8)^{4}}{{sin}^{8}⁡x}(11x+63-8\operatorname{cot}⁡x({x}^{2}+11x+24))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-2+4x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x+1}+4 \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x+1}+4\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x+1}+4)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}:$ 

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{\frac{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}}{\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{1/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{1/2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)-\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{1/2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}\cdot (4{x}^{3}+4x)-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{4{x}^{3}+4x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{2} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{y}{2}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{\frac{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt{\frac{{({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)}^{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{|{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8|}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8>0\text{ }∀x\in R$, so $|{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8|={x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8$ and we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}(\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}+\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}[\frac{8{x}^{3}+8x}{{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8}\cdot ({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)+\operatorname{tan}⁡x({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8)] \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}(8{x}^{3}+8x+\operatorname{tan}⁡x({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+8))\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-254041d3-aef5-5074-80f4-67b8b1344bc0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-b1cca9dd-6ad8-57a8-a947-88e8f34aa52d" :answer-field/id #uuid "b1cca9dd-6ad8-57a8-a947-88e8f34aa52d"] ["answer-419792fe-6389-5363-a771-125381c66945" :answer/id #uuid "419792fe-6389-5363-a771-125381c66945"] ["answer-419792fe-6389-5363-a771-125381c66945" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-419792fe-6389-5363-a771-125381c66945" :answer/value "8x^3+8x"] ["answer-field-b1cca9dd-6ad8-57a8-a947-88e8f34aa52d" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-b1cca9dd-6ad8-57a8-a947-88e8f34aa52d" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-b1cca9dd-6ad8-57a8-a947-88e8f34aa52d" :answer-field/correct "answer-419792fe-6389-5363-a771-125381c66945"] ["answer-field-b1cca9dd-6ad8-57a8-a947-88e8f34aa52d" :answer-field/choices "answer-419792fe-6389-5363-a771-125381c66945"] ["question-254041d3-aef5-5074-80f4-67b8b1344bc0" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-b1cca9dd-6ad8-57a8-a947-88e8f34aa52d"] [17592186064311 :knowledge-point/questions "question-254041d3-aef5-5074-80f4-67b8b1344bc0"] ["question-06abf62c-6dfa-52f6-818c-3858ac967b34" :question/id #uuid "06abf62c-6dfa-52f6-818c-3858ac967b34"] ["question-06abf62c-6dfa-52f6-818c-3858ac967b34" :question/math-academy-id "q-138850"] ["question-06abf62c-6dfa-52f6-818c-3858ac967b34" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.$  The derivative of this function is given by

Find the value of $a+b+c.$"] ["question-06abf62c-6dfa-52f6-818c-3858ac967b34" :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{1/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{1/3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+2x)^{6})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{1/3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2x)+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2x)+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =6\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+2x}\cdot (2x+2)+\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{12(x+1)}{{x}^{2}+2x}+\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{12(x+1)}{{x}^{2}+2x}+\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(\frac{12(x+1)}{{x}^{2}+2x}+\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{3}) \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(\frac{12(x+1)}{{x}^{2}+2x}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡x}) \\  & =({x}^{2}+2x)^{6}\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}(\frac{36(x+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+({x}^{2}+2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{3({x}^{2}+2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡x}) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+2x)^{5}}{3\sqrt[3]{{sin}^{2}⁡x}}((36x+36)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(1{x}^{2}+2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=36+1+2=39.

$y=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}(x-3)^{3}(a{x}^{2}+bx+c).
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$"] ["question-76085196-6a2f-5c76-90cb-5c742aa98a2b" :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}} \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}}\cdot \sqrt{(x-3)^{8}} \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}(x-3)^{8/2} \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}(x-3)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}(x-3)^{4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((x-3)^{4}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-3)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot 2x+4\cdot \frac{1}{x-3} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{3x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{4}{x-3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{3x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{4}{x-3})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}(\frac{3x}{{x}^{2}+1}+\frac{4}{x-3}) \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}(\frac{3x(x-3)+4({x}^{2}+1)}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-3)}) \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}(x-3)^{8}}(\frac{7{x}^{2}-9x+4}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-3)}) \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{3/2}(x-3)^{4}(\frac{7{x}^{2}-9x+4}{({x}^{2}+1)(x-3)}) \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)^{1/2}(x-3)^{3}(7{x}^{2}-9x+4) \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}(x-3)^{3}(7{x}^{2}-9x+4)\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=7+(-9)+4=2.
$$"] ["question-76085196-6a2f-5c76-90cb-5c742aa98a2b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-1d436c14-aa02-5c1c-8f96-e30ae5edad2a" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[4]{\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{(2{x}^{2}+1)^{8}}} \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{(2{x}^{2}+1)^{8}}]}^{1/4} \\  & =({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4}(2{x}^{2}+1)^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4}(2{x}^{2}+1)^{-2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4})+\operatorname{ln}⁡((2{x}^{2}+1)^{-2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+4)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2{x}^{2}+1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\cdot (2x)-2\cdot \frac{1}{2{x}^{2}+1}\cdot (4x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{x}{2({x}^{2}+4)}-\frac{8x}{2{x}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}-\frac{16x}{2{x}^{2}+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{y}{2}(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}-\frac{16x}{2{x}^{2}+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt[4]{\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{(2{x}^{2}+1)^{8}}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt[4]{\frac{{x}^{2}+4}{(2{x}^{2}+1)^{8}}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}-\frac{16x}{2{x}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4}}{2(2{x}^{2}+1)^{2}}(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+4}-\frac{16x}{2{x}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4}}{2(2{x}^{2}+1)^{2}}(\frac{x(2{x}^{2}+1)-16x({x}^{2}+4)}{({x}^{2}+4)(2{x}^{2}+1)}) \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+4)^{1/4}}{2(2{x}^{2}+1)^{2}}(\frac{-14{x}^{3}-63x}{({x}^{2}+4)(2{x}^{2}+1)}) \\  & =-\frac{x(14{x}^{2}+63)}{2(2{x}^{2}+1)^{3}\sqrt[4]{({x}^{2}+4)^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-19b1b664-4a0c-5ebc-8d57-f886d4c9f0c2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-61e10619-0457-5f47-8c3c-d968af092244" :answer-field/id #uuid "61e10619-0457-5f47-8c3c-d968af092244"] ["answer-1424a6ad-ac38-52fa-bea7-f95d3db15e1e" :answer/id #uuid "1424a6ad-ac38-52fa-bea7-f95d3db15e1e"] ["answer-1424a6ad-ac38-52fa-bea7-f95d3db15e1e" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-1424a6ad-ac38-52fa-bea7-f95d3db15e1e" :answer/value "14x^2+63"] ["answer-field-61e10619-0457-5f47-8c3c-d968af092244" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-61e10619-0457-5f47-8c3c-d968af092244" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-61e10619-0457-5f47-8c3c-d968af092244" :answer-field/correct "answer-1424a6ad-ac38-52fa-bea7-f95d3db15e1e"] ["answer-field-61e10619-0457-5f47-8c3c-d968af092244" :answer-field/choices "answer-1424a6ad-ac38-52fa-bea7-f95d3db15e1e"] ["question-19b1b664-4a0c-5ebc-8d57-f886d4c9f0c2" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-61e10619-0457-5f47-8c3c-d968af092244"] [17592186064311 :knowledge-point/questions "question-19b1b664-4a0c-5ebc-8d57-f886d4c9f0c2"] ["question-bc8a78e5-ffc8-5ad6-abfc-11fb82c73f1a" :question/id #uuid "bc8a78e5-ffc8-5ad6-abfc-11fb82c73f1a"] ["question-bc8a78e5-ffc8-5ad6-abfc-11fb82c73f1a" :question/math-academy-id "q-138865"] ["question-bc8a78e5-ffc8-5ad6-abfc-11fb82c73f1a" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{a{x}^{5}+3{x}^{4}+b{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+c}{({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{3/2}\sqrt{{x}^{4}+2x}}.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$"] ["question-bc8a78e5-ffc8-5ad6-abfc-11fb82c73f1a" :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{x}^{4}+2x}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+2x+2}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{4}+2x)^{1/2}}{({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{1/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{({x}^{4}+2x)^{1/2}}{({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{1/2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{4}+2x)^{1/2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{1/2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2x+2)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{4}+2x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2x+2)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{4}+2x}\cdot (4{x}^{3}+2)-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}\cdot (2x+2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{2{x}^{3}+1}{{x}^{4}+2x}-\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{2{x}^{3}+1}{{x}^{4}+2x}-\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+2x+2})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}(\frac{2{x}^{3}+1}{{x}^{4}+2x}-\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}) \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}(\frac{(2{x}^{3}+1)({x}^{2}+2x+2)-(x+1)({x}^{4}+2x)}{({x}^{4}+2x)({x}^{2}+2x+2)}) \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}(\frac{2{x}^{5}+4{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+2x+2-({x}^{5}+{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}+2x)}{({x}^{4}+2x)({x}^{2}+2x+2)}) \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{2}+2x+2}}(\frac{{x}^{5}+3{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+2}{({x}^{4}+2x)({x}^{2}+2x+2)}) \\  & =\frac{1{x}^{5}+3{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+2}{({x}^{2}+2x+2)^{3/2}\sqrt{{x}^{4}+2x}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
a+b+c=1+4+2=7.
$$"] ["question-bc8a78e5-ffc8-5ad6-abfc-11fb82c73f1a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-de6a18ff-6676-56f5-b05e-7d4da313f1e4" :answer-field/id #uuid to find the derivative $y'(x).$ 

For example, consider the following function: 

$$
y = x^2 \cdot 2^x
$$

 

Our goal is to find $y'(x).$ To do this, we will use the product rule for logarithms, namely

$$
\ln(a b)= \ln a + \ln b.
$$

 

We differentiate our function by following four steps.

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the product and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Next, we differentiate both sides of our equation using implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{′}+(x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot \frac{1}{x}+1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Then, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for $y =x^2\cdot 2^x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}(\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =x\cdot {2}^{x+1}+{x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}

$$"] [17592186064760 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] [17592186062617 :answer-field/correct 17592186062622] ["question-89efd351-a602-5741-a803-e137883a9ffc" :question/id #uuid "89efd351-a602-5741-a803-e137883a9ffc"] ["question-89efd351-a602-5741-a803-e137883a9ffc" :question/math-academy-id "q-42784"] ["question-89efd351-a602-5741-a803-e137883a9ffc" :question/problem "$-1+\frac{8}{5}=$"] ["question-89efd351-a602-5741-a803-e137883a9ffc" :question/worked-solution "We put both fractions over a common denominator of $5$ and then add the numerators. This gives

$$
-1+\frac{8}{5}=-\frac{5}{5}+\frac{8}{5}=\frac{-5+8}{5}.
$$

To compute the numerator, we can use either Method 1 or Method 2, shown below.

**Method 1 - Picturing a Number Line**

To add $8$ to $-5,$ we start at $-5$ on a number line and move $8$ spaces to the right.

![](images/0b/0b6274b1cb65e330c81602212fe081835eb86c1c1c8e3a6eee278fbfd2614776.png)

So, $-5+8=3.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{-5+8}{5}=\frac{3}{5}.
$$

**Method 2 - Subtraction in Reverse**

We can swap the order of the numbers in the numerator, and we get

$$
\frac{-5+8}{5}=\frac{8-5}{5}=\frac{3}{5}.
$$

So, we conclude that $-1+\frac{8}{5}=\frac{3}{5}.$"] ["question-89efd351-a602-5741-a803-e137883a9ffc" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-14d93e8f-2ff1-562e-a35c-f8de5c3818d2" :question/problem "$(-5.5)^{2}=$"] ["question-14d93e8f-2ff1-562e-a35c-f8de5c3818d2" :question/worked-solution "We need to calculate the product of $-5.5$ with itself:

$$
(-5.5)^{2}=(-5.5)\cdot (-5.5)=(5.5)\cdot (5.5)
$$

First, we ignore the decimal points and multiply as if both numbers were whole numbers:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} &  &  & \,\,\,\,\begin{aligned}\boxed{2} \\ \boxed{2}\end{aligned}\,\,\,\, &  \\  &  &  & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,\times \,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, \\  &  & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,7\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,+\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,7\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, \\  & \,\,\,\,3\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,2\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\,\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $55\times 55=3\,025.$

We now count the total number of decimal places in the two factors.

There is $1$ decimal place in the first factor ($5.5$) and $1$ decimal place in the second factor ($5.5$), so their product will have $1+1=2$ decimal places.

We take our value of $3\,025$ and insert a decimal point to make a number with $2$ decimal places:

$$
30\,\overset{↓}{.}\,\,\,{{25}_{⏟}}_{2\text{ digits}}
$$

Therefore, ${5.5}^{2}=30.25.$"] ["question-14d93e8f-2ff1-562e-a35c-f8de5c3818d2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-c64d54dd-1bd9-5b4c-bf85-d147344d6818" :answer-field/id $$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=12\,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=12$ and $r=2,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi (2)^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 16\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{4\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem "A spherical hot air balloon is inflated. At a particular moment, the rate of increase in the volume of the balloon is numerically equal to nine-halfs the rate of increase in its surface area. What is the radius of the balloon at that moment?"] ["question-3340fda4-31bb-56af-bac8-5dcbd67440f2" :question/worked-solution "Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon, $V$ the volume, and $A$ its surface area. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the volume $V$ and the surface area $A$ of the sphere. Since $A=4\pi {r}^{2}$ and $V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3},$ the relationship between $V$ and $A$ is

$$
V=\frac{4\pi }{3}{r}^{3}=\frac{4\pi }{3}{(\frac{A}{4\pi })}^{3/2}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{3(4\pi )^{1/2}}=\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}A}(\frac{{A}^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi }}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{2}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{{A}^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi }} \\ {A}^{1/2} & =18\sqrt{\pi } \\ A & ={(18\sqrt{\pi })}^{2} \\ A & =324\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, since $A=4\pi {r}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4\pi {r}^{2} & =324\pi  \\ {r}^{2} & =81 \\ r & =9.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-3340fda4-31bb-56af-bac8-5dcbd67440f2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-893ce6e9-d2a5-5687-890a-43b20d335c93" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-1724c4ea-89ed-51e2-a2bf-8d02f0f074fa" :question/problem "Solve the equation $4{x}^{2}-8x=5.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that ${x}^{2}-2x+1$ is a perfect square.*"] ["question-1724c4ea-89ed-51e2-a2bf-8d02f0f074fa" :question/worked-solution "Using the hint, we have

$$
{x}^{2}-2x+1=(x-1)^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-8x & =5 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2x) & =5 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2\cdot 1x) & =5 \\ 4({x}^{2}-2\cdot 1x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) & =5 \\ 4[(x-1)^{2}-{1}^{2}] & =5 \\ 4[(x-1)^{2}-1] & =5 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-4 & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by adding $4$ to both sides and then dividing by $4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-1)^{2}-4 & =5 \\ 4(x-1)^{2}-4+4 & =5+4 \\ 4(x-1)^{2} & =9 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =\frac{9}{4} \\ \sqrt{(x-1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}} \\ |x-1| & =\frac{3}{2} \\ x-1 & =\pm \frac{3}{2} \\ x & =1\pm \frac{3}{2} \\ x & =-\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}

$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}-18x & =7 \\ 9({x}^{2}-2x) & =7 \\ 9({x}^{2}-2\cdot 1x) & =7 \\ 9({x}^{2}-2\cdot 1y+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) & =7 \\ 9[(x-1)^{2}-{1}^{2}] & =7 \\ 9[(x-1)^{2}-1] & =7 \\ 9(x-1)^{2}-9 & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by adding $9$ to both sides and then dividing by $9$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}9(x-1)^{2}-9 & =7 \\ 9(x-1)^{2}-9+9 & =7+9 \\ 9(x-1)^{2} & =16 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =\frac{16}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =\frac{16}{9} \\ \sqrt{(x-1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{16}{9}} \\ |x-1| & =\frac{4}{3} \\ x-1 & =\pm \frac{4}{3} \\ x & =1\pm \frac{4}{3} \\ x & =-\frac{1}{3},\frac{7}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-cca814ca-cf90-5add-8be7-53a49b278718" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-63bb1ee1-44d2-5a8b-a0ff-8a61b2d8e549" :answer-field/id #uuid in the form $(z+p)^{2}=q.$ Find $\,p+q,$ and solve the equation."] ["question-2236615a-502f-5e6f-8a3b-d0bb2e05f4c6" :question/worked-solution "First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$

$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =4 \\ {(z-\frac{3}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{25}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=-\frac{3}{2},q=\frac{25}{4}$ and $p+q=\frac{19}{4}.$

$$

$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{3}{2}+\frac{5}{2}=4 \\ z & =\frac{3}{2}-\frac{5}{2}=-1\end{aligned}

multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-4{x}^{2}-6x+10) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x-10 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+6x-10 & =0 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x & =10 \\ 4{x}^{2}+6x & =10 \\ 4({x}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}x) & =10 \\ 4[{x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{3}{4}x+{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}] & =10 \\ 4[{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{16}] & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-4\cdot \frac{9}{16} & =10 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}-\frac{9}{4} & =10 \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =10+\frac{9}{4} \\ 4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{49}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{3}{4}.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{49}{4} \\ {(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2} & =\frac{49}{16} \\ \sqrt{{(x+\frac{3}{4})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{49}{16}} \\ |x+\frac{3}{4}| & =\frac{7}{4} \\ x+\frac{3}{4} & =\pm \frac{7}{4} \\ x & =-\frac{3}{4}\pm \frac{7}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{3}{4}-\frac{7}{4}=-\frac{10}{4}=-\frac{5}{2} \\ x & =-\frac{3}{4}+\frac{7}{4}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=-\frac{5}{2}$ and $x=1.$"] ["question-6c6b5462-ae7e-592e-8c21-3452425e7810" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] \begin{aligned}R(t) & =r(t)-8 \\  & =6t+10-8 \\  & =6t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the **total amount of water** after $t$ hours (call it $T(t)$), we apply the second fundamental theorem of calculus:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =T(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}R(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =200+{\int }_{0}^{t}(6x+2)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To ensure that $T$ is a function of $t$ only, we use a different variable ($x$) for the integration. 

To find out the amount of water after $4$ hours ($5\,\text{p.m}$), we substitute $t=4$ into the above and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(4) & =200+{\int }_{0}^{4}(6x+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =200+(3{x}^{2}+2x){|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =200+[(3\cdot 16+8)-0] \\  & =200+56 \\  & =256\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there will be $256$ liters of water in the tank at $5\,\text{p.m}.$"] ["question-b1c05acb-14b2-5a23-a0fb-57fef367611e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-bdb50e03-36f7-5d1f-9178-33250a489690" :answer-field/id #uuid "bdb50e03-36f7-5d1f-9178-33250a489690"] ["answer-e6f34e98-745c-508e-9aac-c7930cd0847b" :answer/id #uuid "e6f34e98-745c-508e-9aac-c7930cd0847b"] ["answer-e6f34e98-745c-508e-9aac-c7930cd0847b" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-e6f34e98-745c-508e-9aac-c7930cd0847b" :answer/value "256"] ["answer-field-bdb50e03-36f7-5d1f-9178-33250a489690" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-bdb50e03-36f7-5d1f-9178-33250a489690" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-bdb50e03-36f7-5d1f-9178-33250a489690" :answer-field/correct "answer-e6f34e98-745c-508e-9aac-c7930cd0847b"] ["answer-field-bdb50e03-36f7-5d1f-9178-33250a489690" :answer-field/choices "answer-e6f34e98-745c-508e-9aac-c7930cd0847b"] ["question-b1c05acb-14b2-5a23-a0fb-57fef367611e" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-bdb50e03-36f7-5d1f-9178-33250a489690"] [17592186147398 :knowledge-point/questions "question-b1c05acb-14b2-5a23-a0fb-57fef367611e"] ["question-7896667b-b339-512f-9dbb-66fd90855442" :question/id #uuid "7896667b-b339-512f-9dbb-66fd90855442"] ["question-7896667b-b339-512f-9dbb-66fd90855442" :question/math-academy-id "q-349984"] ["question-7896667b-b339-512f-9dbb-66fd90855442" :question/problem "A city is tracking the number of bikes available in a bike-share station.

{{field-1}}"] ["question-7896667b-b339-512f-9dbb-66fd90855442" :question/worked-solution "The number of bikes is increasing at a rate of $r(t)$ bikes per hour and is decreasing at a rate of $4$ bikes per hour. Therefore, the **rate of change** $R(t)$ of the number of bikes is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(t) & =r(t)-4 \\  & =5{t}^{3}+2t-4.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the total number $B(t)$ of bikes after $t$ hours, we apply the second fundamental theorem of calculus:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =B(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}R(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =100+{\int }_{0}^{t}(5{x}^{3}+2x-4)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To ensure that our final function is a function of $t$ only, we use a different variable ($x$) for the integration.

We can simplify the expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B(t) & =100+{\int }_{0}^{t}5{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{t}2x\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{0}^{t}4\,\text{d}x \\  & =100+{5\,\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{t}+{2\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{t}-4x{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =100+\frac{5}{4}{t}^{4}+{t}^{2}-4t \\  & =\frac{5}{4}{t}^{4}+\,{t}^{2}-4t+100\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-7896667b-b339-512f-9dbb-66fd90855442" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-9eaf115f-1435-52c2-b951-5e9b2f69cb63" :answer-field/id #uuid "9eaf115f-1435-52c2-b951-5e9b2f69cb63"] ["answer-b9635b2b-705b-58e9-94bd-88166205012c" :answer/id #uuid "b9635b2b-705b-58e9-94bd-88166205012c"] ["answer-b9635b2b-705b-58e9-94bd-88166205012c" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-b9635b2b-705b-58e9-94bd-88166205012c" :answer/value "t^{2}-4t+100"] ["answer-field-9eaf115f-1435-52c2-b951-5e9b2f69cb63" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-9eaf115f-1435-52c2-b951-5e9b2f69cb63" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-9eaf115f-1435-52c2-b951-5e9b2f69cb63" :answer-field/correct "answer-b9635b2b-705b-58e9-94bd-88166205012c"] ["answer-field-9eaf115f-1435-52c2-b951-5e9b2f69cb63" :answer-field/choices "answer-b9635b2b-705b-58e9-94bd-88166205012c"] ["question-7896667b-b339-512f-9dbb-66fd90855442" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-9eaf115f-1435-52c2-b951-5e9b2f69cb63"] [17592186147398 :knowledge-point/questions "question-7896667b-b339-512f-9dbb-66fd90855442"] ["question-54f0409c-f2ef-5cc4-b4e4-ffc38eb896a2" :question/id #uuid "54f0409c-f2ef-5cc4-b4e4-ffc38eb896a2"] ["question-54f0409c-f2ef-5cc4-b4e4-ffc38eb896a2" :question/math-academy-id "q-349997"] ["question-54f0409c-f2ef-5cc4-b4e4-ffc38eb896a2" :question/problem "On a certain afternoon, the total number of people $N(t)$ visiting the city's zoo is given by the function

hours."] ["question-54f0409c-f2ef-5cc4-b4e4-ffc38eb896a2" :question/worked-solution "To find when the number of people at the zoo is at maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}N}{\text{d}t}=0.$ First, we differentiate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}N}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(30+4{\int }_{0}^{t}(10-2x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(30)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{\int }_{0}^{t}(10-2x)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{0}^{t}(10-2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4(10-2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve $\frac{\text{d}N}{\text{d}t}=0$:

$$
4(10-2t)=0\,⟹\,t=5
$$

So there are two candidates for global extrema, $t=0$ and $t=5.$ To find out how many people are in the zoo when $t=5,$ we figure out $N(5):$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(5) & =30+4{\int }_{0}^{5}(10-2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =30+4{[10x-{x}^{2}]|}_{0}^{5} \\  & =30+4[(10\cdot 5-{5}^{2})-(0)] \\  & =30+4\cdot 25 \\  & =130\end{aligned}
$$

Since $30<130$, we conclude that the maximum number of people at the zoo is $130$, and this will happen after $5$ hours."] ["question-54f0409c-f2ef-5cc4-b4e4-ffc38eb896a2" :question/difficulty Given a polygon's vertex, the interior and exterior angles are supplementary. So, for the vertex $B,$ we have:

$$"] [17592186107163 :tutorial/content "Why do the exterior angles of a polygon always sum to $360^\circ?$

Suppose we have an $n$-sided polygon. Then, we have the following:

- There are $n$ pairs of interior-exterior angles, each pair being supplementary (i.e., their measures add to $180^\circ).$

- Therefore, the sum of the measures of *all* interior-exterior pairs equals ${\color{blue}n\cdot 180^\circ}.$

- In a previous lesson, we saw that the sum of the *interior* angles equals ${\color{red}{(n-2)\cdot 180^\circ}}.$

Therefore, to get the sum of the *exterior* angles, we subtract ${\color{red}{(n-2)\cdot 180^\circ}}$ from ${\color{blue}n\cdot 180^\circ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Sum of Exterior Angles} & =n\cdot {180}^{∘}-(n-2)\cdot {180}^{∘} \\  & =n\cdot {180}^{∘}-n\cdot {180}^{∘}+2\cdot {180}^{∘} \\  & =\cancel{n\cdot {180}^{∘}}-\cancel{n\cdot {180}^{∘}}+2\cdot {180}^{∘} \\  & =2\cdot {180}^{∘} \\  & ={360}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

This proves that the sum of the exterior angles of a (simple) polygon equals $360^\circ.$"] [17592186105975 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0] ["answer-d5430906-9808-587e-9c79-133123248909" :answer/id #uuid "d5430906-9808-587e-9c79-133123248909"] ["answer-d5430906-9808-587e-9c79-133123248909" :answer/type :answer.type/text] ["answer-d5430906-9808-587e-9c79-133123248909" :answer/value ">"] [17592186478315 :answer-field/correct "answer-d5430906-9808-587e-9c79-133123248909"] [17592186478315 :answer-field/choices "answer-d5430906-9808-587e-9c79-133123248909"] ["question-38e098ba-2563-5c51-8af3-272acb29f55b" :question/id #uuid "38e098ba-2563-5c51-8af3-272acb29f55b"] ["question-38e098ba-2563-5c51-8af3-272acb29f55b" :question/math-academy-id "q-277800"] ["question-38e098ba-2563-5c51-8af3-272acb29f55b" :question/problem "From **left to right,** the $x$-intercepts of the hyperbola $9{x}^{2}-16{y}^{2}=144$ are

Our goal is to find $y'(x)$. To do this, we will use the product rule for logarithms, namely

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the product and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ln y &= \ln (x^{2} \cdot 2^{x}) \\
\ln y &= \ln (x^{2}) + \ln (2^{x}) \\
\ln y &= 2\ln x + x\ln 2
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Next, we differentiate both sides of our equation using implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\ln y) &= \frac{d}{dx}(2\ln x + x\ln 2) \\

\frac{1}{y} \cdot y^{′} &= 2 \cdot \frac{1}{x} + 1 \cdot \ln (2) \\
\frac{y^{′}}{y} &= \frac{2}{x} + \ln 2
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Then, we solve for $y'{:}$

\begin{aligned}

Given a polygon's vertex, the interior and exterior angles are supplementary. So, for the vertex $B$, we have:

$$
\underbrace{\color{YellowOrange}m\angle{ABC}}_{\large\text{Interior}} \:+\: \underbrace{\color{blue}m\angle{CBE}}_{\large\text{Exterior}} = 180^\circ
$$

We have the following theorem:

> The measures of the exterior angles of any simple polygon sum to $360^\circ$.

We'll show why this theorem is true at the end of the lesson.

$$

$$"] [17592186107163 :tutorial/content "Why do the exterior angles of a polygon always sum to $360^\circ$?

Suppose we have an $n$-sided polygon. Then, we have the following:

- There are $n$ pairs of interior-exterior angles, each pair being supplementary (i.e., their measures add to $180^\circ)$.
- Therefore, the sum of the measures of *all* interior-exterior pairs equals ${\color{blue}n\cdot 180^\circ}$.
- In a previous lesson, we saw that the sum of the *interior* angles equals ${\color{red}{(n-2)\cdot 180^\circ}}$.

Therefore, to get the sum of the *exterior* angles, we subtract ${\color{red}{(n-2)\cdot 180^\circ}}$ from ${\color{blue}n\cdot 180^\circ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Sum of Exterior Angles &= n \cdot 180^{∘} - (n - 2) \cdot 180^{∘} \\
&= n \cdot 180^{∘} - n \cdot 180^{∘} + 2 \cdot 180^{∘} \\

There should be no powers on any of the variables and the variables can't be multiplied together.

For example, the following are linear equations:

$$
y = x + 4, \qquad
	y = -3x, \qquad
	5y = 6x,\qquad
	2x + 3y = 9
$$

On the other hand, the following are *not* linear equations:

$$
y = x^2 - 2x, \qquad
	y^2 = - 4x + 2, \qquad
	y = 2xy
$$

A **solution** of a linear equation is an **ordered pair** $(x,y)$ that makes the equation true. 

For instance, the ordered pair $(3, 7)$ is a solution to the equation $y = 3x - 2$ because if we replace $x$ with $3$ and $y$ with $7,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x-2 \\ (7) & =3(3)-2 \\ 7 & =9-2 \\ 7 & =7\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

The above is a true statement, so $(3, 7)$ is a solution to the equation $y = 3x - 2.$

**Important**: A linear equation in two variables has an infinite number of solutions, not just one!" :tutorial/id #uuid "c51c3f80-5dd0-5f6e-a939-4d11e9f42c71" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1434 $$
\dfrac{(y-k)^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{(x-h)^2}{b^2}=1.
$$

To rewrite the equation of the hyperbola in the above form, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{y}^{2}-10{x}^{2}-8y-40x & =76 \\ 4{y}^{2}-8y-10{x}^{2}-40x & =76 \\ 4[{y}^{2}-2y]-10[{x}^{2}+4x] & =76 \\ 4[(y-1)^{2}-1]-10[(x+2)^{2}-4] & =76 \\ 4(y-1)^{2}-4-10(x+2)^{2}+40 & =76 \\ 4(y-1)^{2}-10(x+2)^{2} & =76-40+4 \\ 4(y-1)^{2}-10(x+2)^{2} & =40 \\ \frac{(y-1)^{2}}{10}-\frac{(x+2)^{2}}{4} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$6{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}+48x-48y=72?$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of a horizontal hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

To rewrite the equation of the hyperbola in the above form, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}^{2}-4{y}^{2}+48x-48y & =72 \\ 6{x}^{2}+48x-4{y}^{2}-48y & =72 \\ 6[{x}^{2}+8x]-4[{y}^{2}+12y] & =72 \\ 6[(x+4)^{2}-16]-4[(y+6)^{2}-36] & =72 \\ 6(x+4)^{2}-96-4(y+6)^{2}+144 & =72 \\ 6(x+4)^{2}-4(y+6)^{2} & =24 \\ \frac{(x+4)^{2}}{4}-\frac{(y+6)^{2}}{6} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-(-4))^{2}}{{2}^{2}}-\frac{(y-(-6))^{2}}{(\sqrt{6})^{2}} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the center is $(-4,-6).$"} {:db/id 17592186250531 :question/id #uuid "55d78d11-140f-535d-9e65-7b7af7dfd48e" :question/math-academy-id "q-116113"} {:db/id 17592186292766 :question/id #uuid "aed0176b-d065-50a3-b46b-f8eb6c3a9ebb" :question/math-academy-id "q-274638"} {:db/id 17592186302429 :question/id #uuid "09c925d6-50d3-5bb2-a85f-2c23d9456fed" :question/math-academy-id "q-328353"} {:db/id 17592186302430 :question/id #uuid "d8162c3a-d644-506a-968b-c4b5bfa37969" :question/math-academy-id "q-328355"} {:db/id 17592186302431 :question/id #uuid "732ba5f4-6963-5996-99c9-00c1b82bcf8f" :question/math-academy-id "q-328358"} {:db/id 17592186302436 :question/id #uuid "2d46bedb-abf3-5e0e-be7c-58482d588bb6" :question/math-academy-id "q-328374"} {:db/id 17592186302437 :question/id #uuid "6bc48671-a72b-5e74-a845-63b61e701b90" :question/math-academy-id "q-328382"} {:db/id 17592186304771 :question/id #uuid "9a7281ca-5d52-5291-98ac-5167d073adb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-328439"} {:db/id 17592186348117 :question/id #uuid "772bbeac-04ec-54bd-9642-971cce1dc84c" :question/math-academy-id "q-78870"} {:db/id 17592186348118 :question/id #uuid "209d3fb4-3f5a-5f61-958c-85386d790787" :question/math-academy-id "q-78871"} {:db/id 17592186348119 :question/id #uuid "70880c3d-4012-5cf5-bf26-9498ab363505" :question/math-academy-id "q-78872"} {:db/id 17592186364873 :question/id #uuid "f2bde32f-6c1a-5f51-a9db-63442e278458" :question/math-academy-id "q-116112"} {:db/id 17592186365594 :question/id #uuid "88f28c66-d759-5b8d-b8f7-f31f33a24401" :question/math-academy-id "q-328436"} {:db/id 17592186366330 :question/id #uuid "1dacb1be-8b20-5565-8b5e-13ef56b8965e" :question/math-academy-id "q-78874"} {:db/id 17592186049029} {:db/id 17592186050123} {:db/id 17592186050863} {:db/id 17592186051028 :topic/difficulty 0.7689827632703577 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186429672 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. $$

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform $L$ to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a system with variables ${X}_{1}(s)=L{{x}_{1}(t)}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L{{x}_{2}(t)}.$ In terms of the parameter $s,$ the solution of the new system is

${X}_{1}(s)=$ {{field-1}},$\,$
${X}_{2}(s)=\frac{s+2}{s(s-5)}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}L{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)}=L{2{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t)} \\ L{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)}=L{5{x}_{2}(t)+2}\end{aligned}\,\,
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}sL{{x}_{1}(t)}-{x}_{1}(0)=2L{{x}_{1}(t)}+3L{{x}_{2}(t)} \\ sL{{x}_{2}(t)}-{x}_{2}(0)=5L{{x}_{2}(t)}+2L{1}\end{aligned}
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-0=2{X}_{1}(s)+3{X}_{2}(s) \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-1=5{X}_{2}(s)+\frac{2}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L{{x}_{1}(t)}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L{{x}_{2}(t)},$ and we have used the fact that $L{1}=\frac{1}{s}.$

Now, solving the second equation for ${X}_{2}(s),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{2}(s)-1 & =5{X}_{2}(s)+\frac{2}{s} \\ (s-5){X}_{2}(s) & =1+\frac{2}{s} \\ (s-5){X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{s+2}{s} \\ {X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{s+2}{s(s-5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this in the first equation and solving for ${X}_{1}(s)$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s) & =2{X}_{1}(s)+3{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s-2){X}_{1}(s) & =3{X}_{2}(s) \\ (s-2){X}_{1}(s) & =3(\frac{s+2}{s(s-5)}) \\ {X}_{1}(s) & =\frac{3(s+2)}{s(s-5)(s-2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution of the new system in terms of parameter $s$ is 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=\frac{3(s+2)}{s(s-2)(s-5)},\,{X}_{2}(s)=\frac{s+2}{s(s-5)}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308370 :question/id #uuid "674fd557-087f-5021-90ca-9f059df8fea3" :question/math-academy-id "q-333071"} {:db/id 17592186308371 :question/id #uuid Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a transformed system with the solution 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=L{{x}_{1}(t)}=\frac{1}{s-1}-\frac{3}{s},\,{X}_{2}(s)=L{{x}_{2}(t)}=\frac{1/2}{s-1}-\frac{1}{s}+\frac{3/2}{s-3}.
$$

Find the solution to the original initial value problem.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}{{X}_{1}(s)} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-1}-\frac{3}{s}} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-1}}-3{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s}} \\  & ={e}^{1\cdot t}-3\cdot 1 \\  & ={e}^{t}-3 \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}{{X}_{2}(s)} \\  & ={L}^{-1}{\frac{1/2}{s-1}-\frac{1}{s}+\frac{3/2}{s-3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-1}}-{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s}}+\frac{3}{2}{L}^{-1}{\frac{1}{s-3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{1\cdot t}-1+\frac{3}{2}{e}^{3\cdot t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{t}+\frac{3}{2}{e}^{3t}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}-3 \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{t}+\frac{3}{2}{e}^{3t}-1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167233 :question/id #uuid "63d4e608-bf55-5ffd-acb6-0fb6294a7841" :question/math-academy-id "q-333131"} {:db/id 17592186308390 :question/id #uuid
