17592186120018} {:db/id 17592186120715 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121050 :tutorial/content "If we are given an equation of a plane using the dot product, we can always obtain an equation in terms of $x,$ $y,$ and $z.$ For example, suppose we have the plane that passes through the point $P(-7,5,-2)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{n}=\langle 3,-6,5 \rangle.$

First, we note that the position vector of the point $P$ is $\mathbf{p}=\langle -7,5,-2 \rangle,$ and we can write down the equation of the plane using the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨3,-6,5⟩ & =⟨-7,5,-2⟩\cdot ⟨3,-6,5⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨3,-6,5⟩ & =-61\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation, we substitute $\mathbf{r}=\langle x,y,z \rangle$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨3,-6,5⟩ & =-61 \\ 3x-6y+5z & =-61 \\ 3x-6y+5z+61 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This final equation is called the **Cartesian equation of the plane**.

![](images/77/77f18981dda500889655225eabbec730b7b295e6b16cec1700d56c2e27e0ac91.png)

Note that in the equation 

$$
{\color{blue}3}x+({\color{blue}-6})y+{\color{blue}5}z+61 = 0,
$$

the coefficients next to $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ are the coordinates of the normal vector 

$$
\mathbf{n}=\langle {\color{blue}3},{\color{blue}-6},{\color{blue}5} \rangle
$$

the line 
$\frac{x-2}{-1}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+1}{1}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that the position vector of $P$ is $p=⟨1,-1,1⟩.$ From the canonical equation, we find that the line is parallel to the vector $⟨-1,2,1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of the plane is 

$$
n=⟨-1,2,1⟩.
$$

Using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-1,2,1⟩ & =⟨1,-1,1⟩\cdot ⟨-1,2,1⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-1,2,1⟩ & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute $r=⟨x,y,z⟩$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨-1,2,1⟩ & =-2 \\ -x+2y+z & =-2 \\ -x+2y+z+2 & =0 \\ x-2y-z-2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4426cd88-0ed0-5a8a-bd40-151d1e9d59dd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186419428}} {:db/id 17592186419425 :step/content {:db/id 17592186419421 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "66b70f6a-e851-54e5-aa28-b6a025e9ece5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "57" :db/id 17592186419408}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186419408} :answer-field/id #uuid "2f1bb041-bd3b-51ec-95b9-ab27a720aff3" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186419416} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b0061273-aae7-5a50-ba3b-7dbc44ba608c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186419411}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186419411} :answer-field/id #uuid "51f6537d-feab-5ce3-9fc6-f89624d037a2" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186419418} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "373d6628-e7af-5c99-8ea7-bda3f45e1294" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186419407}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186419407} :answer-field/id #uuid "c79424ce-ee00-57d0-b195-b7db6dde7351" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186419420}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "53aad395-ec2e-5a47-9cdb-e404625e4482" :question/math-academy-id "q-330576" :question/problem "Find a Cartesian equation of the plane that passes through the point $P(7,4,-3)$ and is perpendicular to the line

$$

Using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨5,4,-2⟩ & =⟨7,4,-3⟩\cdot ⟨5,4,-2⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨5,4,-2⟩ & =57\end{aligned}

Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute $r=⟨x,y,z⟩$ into the equation above and get

Now, we solve the Cartesian equation of $Π$ for $z$:

$$
\begin{aligned}12y-6z-30 & =0 \\ -6z & =-12y+30 \\ z & =2y-5\end{aligned}

First, using the $3$ points we build $2$ vectors parallel to the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} & =\overset{\to }{AP} \\  & =⟨3,-4,1⟩-⟨1,-2,0⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-2,1⟩ \\ {v}_{2} & =\overset{\to }{AQ} \\  & =⟨2,1,-2⟩-⟨1,-2,0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,3,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$

that the position vectors of the points $A,P$ and $Q$ are $a=⟨1,-2,0⟩,\,p=⟨3,-4,1⟩,$ and $q=⟨2,1,-2⟩.$

First, using the $3$ points we build $2$ vectors parallel to the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} & =\overset{\to }{AP} \\  & =⟨3,-4,1⟩-⟨1,-2,0⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-2,1⟩ \\ {v}_{2} & =\overset{\to }{AQ} \\  & =⟨2,1,-2⟩-⟨1,-2,0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,3,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find the normal vector of the plane. To do that, we use the cross product of ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & ={v}_{1}\times {v}_{2} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\times [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =i+5j+8k \\  & =⟨1,5,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨1,5,8⟩ & =⟨3,-4,1⟩\cdot ⟨1,5,8⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨1,5,8⟩ & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute $r=⟨x,y,z⟩$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨1,5,8⟩ & =-9 \\ x+5y+8z & =-9 \\ x+5y+8z+9 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6d308039-35f2-59e5-b262-324c1a8c2bf2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186419425}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "102de1fa-9039-5418-a721-6fc419237fc4" :answer/type {:db/id $$

$$

\begin{aligned}n & ={v}_{1}\times {v}_{2} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\times [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =2i+3j \\  & =⟨2,3,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨2,3,0⟩ & =⟨2,0,-3⟩\cdot ⟨2,3,0⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨2,3,0⟩ & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute $r=⟨x,y,z⟩$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨2,3,0⟩ & =4 \\ 2x+3y & =4 \\ 2x+3y-4 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "24b7f863-ce6a-5264-b6ec-ac8e65ecdb05"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10191765-520e-51b1-b616-6aed299a1951" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value :question/math-academy-id "q-70819" :question/problem "Given the Cartesian equation $x-2y+3z=0$ of the plane $Π$, find an equation of $Π$ in the form $(r-p)\cdot n=0.$" :question/worked-solution "First, from the equation of the plane we get that the normal vector of $Π$ is $n=⟨1,-2,3⟩.$

Now, we solve the Cartesian equation of $Π$ for $z$:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2y+3z & =0 \\ 3z & =-x+2y \\ z & =-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{2}{3}y.\end{aligned}
$$

If we put, say, $x=0$ and $y=0$, we get $z=0.$ Hence, the point $P(0,0,0)$ lies on $Π.$ Note that the position vector of $P$ is $p=⟨0,0,0⟩.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ (r-⟨0,0,0⟩)\cdot ⟨1,-2,3⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "eee37068-88fb-59e1-930d-db5693058840" :step/next {:db/id 17592186423961}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "13bd6234-56f6-541c-bfc5-f390a8cb5bfa" :answer/type {:db/id :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186084061 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084526 :tutorial/content "Let's plot the graph of

$$
y= \mid x \mid
$$

. According to the algebraic definition of absolute value, we have

$$
{x\begin{vmatrix}forx \ge 0 \\ -x\end{vmatrix}forx < 0
$$

So, the left-hand branch of the graph is the function $y=-x$, and the right-hand branch is $y=x$:

![](images/60/60ad4dfdb6086f20f5137c5b4ac4905e55d5697ec4cf31575bf79be5fd408e0c.png)

Notice that the graph has a sharp corner at $(0,0)$. We call this point the **vertex** or the **minimum point.**

We can apply **horizontal** and **vertical translations** to the graph of

$$
y= \mid x \mid
$$

.

- The graph of $y= \mid x \mid +a$ is a **vertical translation** of the absolute value graph $y= \mid x \mid$. It moves the graph $a$ units up.![](images/bc/bc56f0d75b8359f71a104580902a18a1d8009091b94694beb7f8ac71c9bfc9bc.png)
- The graph of $y= \mid x-a \mid$ is a **horizontal translation** of the absolute value graph $y= \mid x \mid$. It moves the graph $a$ units to the *right*.![](images/1f/1f79063f7350e734811366545507fc44c321882d2d9b228b85475a27d46c1759.png)

Note the following:

- When drawing horizontal and vertical translations, it is easiest to transform the graph's vertex first. Then, the two branches can be drawn coming out of the vertex.
- When we translate the graph $y= \mid x \mid$, the resulting curve is called the **image** of $y = \mid x \mid$ under the translation." :tutorial/id #uuid "1b8dce6a-8742-581b-80f6-e39c9943b395" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9295 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "bdb8f706-56c3-508a-a745-c4cf4b268e01" :step/math-academy-id 169443 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084062}} {:db/id 17592186084062 :step/content {:db/id 17592186083189 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186082947 :question/id #uuid "5a2db9be-6ef3-5466-a7cc-4e7e2b5670ec" :question/math-academy-id "e-14919"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "61ec00a6-06ae-5d78-bb1a-b06351432cc3" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049534} {:db/id 17592186049844}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186083554} {:db/id 17592186083623}] :knowledge-point/title "Graphing a Vertical Translation"} :step/id #uuid "6d0878f5-845c-5163-b1ae-e72f37806b6d" :step/math-academy-id 169444 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084063}} {:db/id 17592186084063 :step/content {:db/id 17592186083190 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186082948 :question/id #uuid "2e688f8d-16cc-58d6-8791-538cc335ce04" :question/math-academy-id "e-14925"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "05cffafa-cfcf-5979-a413-b7d0b66dd434" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186083624} {:db/id 17592186083676}] :knowledge-point/title "Graphing a Horizontal Translation"} :step/id #uuid "dfd03723-b5ce-5ca8-98bb-2b1cf56700d6" :step/math-academy-id 169447 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084064}} {:db/id 17592186084064 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084528 :tutorial/content "Horizontal and vertical translations can be combined. ![](images/1d/1dbe4c3e8ea97c0ac077c37143802366c5817d86965ab1dbc5abf54cd01d27c3.png)

Let's look at some examples.

- A **trapezoid** is a quadrilateral with exactly ![](images/95/95836ae470c61ab15bfb67d6f0c92d2ad8d03d400b04473e81e58de3ee44bf32.svg) pair of opposite sides that are parallel to each other. 
The parallel sides are called the **bases**. The other two sides are called the **legs**.

![](images/9f/9fa09c46a2119d35c796065a696954931e20062fd5b3677a5484bef92bc2b0d8.png)

- An **isosceles trapezoid** is a  trapezoid with congruent legs.

![](images/b6/b6b2b2012c1d724f9da8b23551ec4f978f190d86875d7db7a3074635d7f40c02.png)

- A **parallelogram** is a quadrilateral with ![](images/f5/f5f3224583db57b9cfe323c8489ef5e5271000002b5ea253eb98fd067a858b2d.svg) pairs of parallel sides.

 

![](images/5d/5d0f383f3510f54b415a7ab99ef52fb30270924f97b8afec59534a96cd3edcef.png)

 Opposite sides and opposite angles of a parallelogram are always congruent. Moreover, if a quadrilateral has ![](images/f5/f5f3224583db57b9cfe323c8489ef5e5271000002b5ea253eb98fd067a858b2d.svg) pairs of opposite congruent sides or  ![](images/f5/f5f3224583db57b9cfe323c8489ef5e5271000002b5ea253eb98fd067a858b2d.svg) pairs of opposite congruent angles, it is always a parallelogram.

![](images/39/39ccf26333785f9ef47eed68a96bc40005a6ba025fdb6e250beefe14f10b043d.png)

- A **rectangle** is a parallelogram where all angles are right.

 

![](images/55/55a16e0ba93bf1f01d576cca558805aaea9631d1fa8e43b149509d4f8eb4c834.png)

 A rectangle where all sides are congruent is a **square**.

![](images/a0/a04b2a0e86be8b085c5e3fc906d5aa66dfea45c033d52cd4746031202a7d427d.png)

- A **rhombus** is a parallelogram where all sides are congruent. The opposite angles of a rhombus are also congruent.

![](images/d3/d3588d7cbe8f285198df3909df3c03fdec04f53a3f75769e46a0ab4283fa27b3.png)

 A rhombus where all angles are congruent is a **square**.

 

![](images/94/941872050d5407bcd9cb532e318276adccff802230ed854a2d292666fc0096fc.png)

- A **kite** is a quadrilateral with two pairs of congruent sides that are adjacent to each other.

"Consider the function $y = x^5 (\cos x)^x$. Its derivative is given by

$y'(x) = x^4 (\cos x)^x \left(5 + g(x) \right)$.

Find the function $g(x)$." :question/worked-solution "We have the function

$$
y = x^5 (\cos x)^x
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ln y &= \ln (x^{5}(\cos x)^{x}) \\
\ln y &= \ln (x^{5}) + \ln ((\cos x)^{x}) \\
\ln y &= 5\ln x + x\ln (\cos x)
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\ln y) &= \frac{d}{dx}(5\ln x + x\ln (\cos x)) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot y^{′} &= \frac{5}{x} + (x)^{′} \cdot \ln (\cos x) + x \cdot (\ln (\cos x))^{′} \\
\frac{y^{′}}{y} &= \frac{5}{x} + \ln (\cos x) + x \cdot \frac{1}{\cos x} \cdot (-\sin x) \\
\frac{y^{′}}{y} &= \frac{5}{x} + \ln (\cos x) - x\tan x
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= y(\frac{5}{x} + \ln (\cos x) - x\tan x)
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute

$$
y = x^5 (\cos x)^x {:}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= x^{5}(\cos x)^{x}(\frac{5}{x} + \ln (\cos x) - x\tan x) \\
&= x^{5}(\cos x)^{x}(\frac{5}{x} + (x\ln (\cos x))/(x) - \frac{x^{2}\tan x}{x}) \\
&= x^{4}(\cos x)^{x}(5 + x ln ⁡ (cos ⁡ x) - x 2 tan ⁡ x)
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(x) = x \ln (\cos x) - x^2 \tan x
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048773} {:db/id 17592186050375} {:db/id 17592186064655 :question/id #uuid "20a19816-3778-50bd-b683-988f1999abb1" :question/math-academy-id "q-2539"} {:db/id 17592186064662 :question/id #uuid "e94c1f74-7143-5925-b087-ccc750556a18" :question/math-academy-id "q-2568"} {:db/id 17592186064310 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064147 :question/id #uuid "7db11c8c-344b-5d87-a8ae-3b006e5bd92b" :question/math-academy-id "e-9846"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "71dd9228-4b05-54d9-aeb2-3bdabf89e0e9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049079} {:db/id 17592186050542}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064653 :question/id #uuid "66a9a7fc-2bdb-5293-8ab8-3fffc2746847" :question/math-academy-id "q-2537"} {:db/id 17592186064663 :question/id #uuid "c39309cf-bcea-5322-95d0-d9e4a6d81347" :question/math-academy-id "q-2570"}] :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating a Quotient"} {:db/id 17592186064147 :question/id #uuid "7db11c8c-344b-5d87-a8ae-3b006e5bd92b" :question/math-academy-id "e-9846" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186064310 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "71dd9228-4b05-54d9-aeb2-3bdabf89e0e9" :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating a Quotient"}] :question/problem "Consider the function $y = \dfrac{(x+3)^3}{(x+5)^6}$. The derivative of this function is given by
$y' = -\dfrac{g(x)(x+3)^2}{(x+5)^7}$.

Find the function $g(x)$." :question/worked-solution "We have the function

$$
y = \dfrac{(x+3)^3}{(x+5)^6}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ln y &= \ln (((x + 3)^{3})/((x + 5)^{6})) \\
\ln y &= \ln ((x + 3)^{3}) - \ln ((x + 5)^{6}) \\
\ln y &= 3\ln (x + 3) - 6\ln (x + 5)
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\ln y) &= \frac{d}{dx}(3\ln (x + 3) - 6\ln (x + 5)) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot y^{′} &= 3 \cdot \frac{1}{x + 3} - 6 \cdot \frac{1}{x + 5} \\
\frac{y^{′}}{y} &= \frac{3}{x + 3} - \frac{6}{x + 5}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= y(\frac{3}{x + 3} - \frac{6}{x + 5})
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute

$$
y = \dfrac{(x+3)^3}{(x+5)^6}{:}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= ((x + 3)^{3})/((x + 5)^{6})(\frac{3}{x + 3} - \frac{6}{x + 5}) \\
&= ((x + 3)^{3})/((x + 5)^{6})((3(x + 5) - 6(x + 3))/((x + 3)(x + 5))) \\
&= ((x + 3)^{3})/((x + 5)^{6})((-3x - 3)/((x + 3)(x + 5))) \\
&= - (3 (x + 1)(x + 3)^{2})/((x + 5)^{7})
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(x) = \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{3(x+1)}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049079} {:db/id 17592186050542} {:db/id 17592186064653 :question/id #uuid "66a9a7fc-2bdb-5293-8ab8-3fffc2746847" :question/math-academy-id "q-2537"} {:db/id 17592186064663 :question/id #uuid "c39309cf-bcea-5322-95d0-d9e4a6d81347" :question/math-academy-id "q-2570"} {:db/id 17592186064311 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064148 :question/id #uuid "e0cec84d-96cf-5fed-ba05-a5cfc57841a1" :question/math-academy-id "e-9847"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c6005f9a-3eba-5f8d-909d-894d9cd24d12" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050208} {:db/id 17592186050496} {:db/id 17592186050887} {:db/id 17592186050894}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064652 :question/id #uuid "27e870f5-3e1e-55e7-9174-58f13ed02354" :question/math-academy-id "q-2536"} {:db/id 17592186064654 :question/id #uuid "e7fc1f62-d0f6-5f97-ba6d-abeadc5dcf60" :question/math-academy-id "q-2538"} {:db/id 17592186233441 :question/id #uuid "3ac66977-fb7e-55ea-b01a-306cc1fa6e11" :question/math-academy-id "q-138848"}] :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating a Radical Expression"} {:db/id 17592186064148 :question/id #uuid "e0cec84d-96cf-5fed-ba05-a5cfc57841a1" :question/math-academy-id "e-9847" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186064311 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c6005f9a-3eba-5f8d-909d-894d9cd24d12" :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating a Radical Expression"}] :question/problem "Consider the function $y = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{x^2}{x^5+ 1}}$. The derivative of this function is given by
$y' = \dfrac{g(x)}{3\sqrt[3]{x(x^5+1)^4}}$.

Find the function $g(x)$." :question/worked-solution "Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= \sqrt[3]{\frac{x^{2}}{x^{5} + 1}} \\
&= \frac{\sqrt[3]{x^{2}}}{\sqrt[3]{x^{5} + 1}} \\
&= (x^{2/3})/((x^{5} + 1)^{1/3})
\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ln y &= \ln ((x^{2/3})/((x^{5} + 1)^{1/3})) \\
\ln y &= \ln (x^{2/3}) - \ln ((x^{5} + 1)^{1/3}) \\
\ln y &= \frac{2}{3}\ln x - \frac{1}{3}\ln (x^{5} + 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\ln y) &= \frac{d}{dx}(\frac{2}{3}\ln x - \frac{1}{3}\ln (x^{5} + 1)) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot y^{′} &= \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{x^{5} + 1} \cdot (5x^{4}) \\
\frac{y^{′}}{y} &= \frac{1}{3}(\frac{2}{x} - \frac{5x^{4}}{x^{5} + 1})
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= y(\frac{1}{3}(\frac{2}{x} - \frac{5x^{4}}{x^{5} + 1}))
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute

$$
y = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{x^2}{x^5+ 1}}{:}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= \frac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{\frac{x^{2}}{x^{5} + 1}}(\frac{2}{x} - \frac{5x^{4}}{x^{5} + 1}) \\
&= \frac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{\frac{x^{2}}{x^{5} + 1}}((2(x^{5} + 1) - 5x^{5})/(x(x^{5} + 1))) \\
&= \frac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{\frac{x^{2}}{x^{5} + 1}}((-3x^{5} + 2)/(x(x^{5} + 1))) \\
&= \frac{1}{3}\sqrt[3]{\frac{x^{2}}{x^{5} + 1}}((-3x^{5} + 2)/(\sqrt[3]{x^{3}(x^{5} + 1)^{3}})) \\
&= (-3 x 5 + 2)/(3\sqrt[3]{x(x^{5} + 1)^{4}})
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(x) = \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{-3x^5+2}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050208} {:db/id 17592186050496} {:db/id 17592186050887} {:db/id 17592186050894} {:db/id 17592186064652 :question/id #uuid "27e870f5-3e1e-55e7-9174-58f13ed02354" :question/math-academy-id "q-2536"} {:db/id 17592186064654 :question/id #uuid "e7fc1f62-d0f6-5f97-ba6d-abeadc5dcf60" :question/math-academy-id "q-2538"} {:db/id 17592186233441 :question/id #uuid "3ac66977-fb7e-55ea-b01a-306cc1fa6e11" :question/math-academy-id "q-138848"} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186065206} :activity/id #uuid "4dd7be6e-e9a7-53a7-9076-0bf7c12d09ee" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048919 :topic/id #uuid "cc7fb2dc-62dc-56f4-976f-30935824115a" :topic/math-academy-id 344} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186065206 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065396 :tutorial/content "When a function $y=y(x)$ contains complex products, quotients, or radicals, we can use logarithmic differentiation to find the derivative $y'(x)$.

For example, consider the following function:

$$
y = x^2 \cdot 2^x
$$

Our goal is to find $y'(x)$. To do this, we will use the product rule for logarithms, namely

$$
\ln(a b)= \ln a + \ln b
$$

We differentiate our function by following four steps.

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the product and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ln y &= \ln (x^{2} \cdot 2^{x}) \\
\ln y &= \ln (x^{2}) + \ln (2^{x}) \\
\ln y &= 2\ln x + x\ln 2
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Next, we differentiate both sides of our equation using implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\ln y) &= \frac{d}{dx}(2\ln x + x\ln 2) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot y^{′} &= 2 \cdot (\ln x)^{′} + (x)^{′} \cdot \ln (2) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot y^{′} &= 2 \cdot \frac{1}{x} + 1 \cdot \ln (2) \\
\frac{y^{′}}{y} &= \frac{2}{x} + \ln 2
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Then, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= y(\frac{2}{x} + \ln 2)
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for

$$
y =x^2\cdot 2^x{:}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= x^{2} \cdot 2^{x}(\frac{2}{x} + \ln 2) \\
&= x \cdot 2^{x + 1} + x^{2} \cdot 2^{x}\ln 2
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1895a7f3-5ba4-5a31-85b3-6a7b050b307c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6088 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "caef414d-4f2a-5504-9b92-39a03d2f3c8f" :step/math-academy-id :step/math-academy-id 37038} {:db/id 17592186065210 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065397 :tutorial/content "In cases where we wish to differentiate a quotient of functions

$$
y = f(x) = \dfrac{g(x)}{h(x)}
$$

we can apply the quotient rule for logarithms:

$$
\ln \left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right) = \ln a - \ln b
$$

For example, let's compute $y'$, where the function $y$ is given by

$$
y = \dfrac {e^{x^2}}{(1-2x)^2(x-1)^3}
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ln y &= \ln ((e^{x^{2}})/((1 - 2x)^{2}(x - 1)^{3})) \\
\ln y &= \ln (e^{x^{2}}) - \ln ((1 - 2x)^{2}) - \ln ((x - 1)^{3}) \\
\ln y &= x^{2} - 2\ln (1 - 2x) - 3\ln (x - 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\ln y) &= \frac{d}{dx}(x^{2} - 2\ln (1 - 2x) - 3\ln (x - 1)) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot y^{′} &= 2x - 2 \cdot \frac{1}{1 - 2x} \cdot (-2) - 3 \cdot \frac{1}{x - 1} \\
\frac{y^{′}}{y} &= 2x + \frac{4}{1 - 2x} - \frac{3}{x - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= y(2x + \frac{4}{1 - 2x} - \frac{3}{x - 1})
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute our expression for $y$, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= (e^{x^{2}})/((1 - 2x)^{2}(x - 1)^{3})(2x + \frac{4}{1 - 2x} - \frac{3}{x - 1}) \\
&= (e^{x^{2}})/((1 - 2x)^{2}(x - 1)^{3})((2x(1 - 2x)(x - 1) + 4(x - 1) - 3(1 - 2x))/((1 - 2x)(x - 1))) \\
&= (e^{x^{2}})/((1 - 2x)^{3}(x - 1)^{4})(2x(1 - 2x)(x - 1) + 4(x - 1) - 3(1 - 2x)) \\
&= (e^{x^{2}})/((1 - 2x)^{3}(x - 1)^{4})(-4x^{3} + 6x^{2} + 8x - 7) \\
&= - (e^{x^{2}})/((1 - 2x)^{3}(x - 1)^{4})(4x^{3} - 6x^{2} - 8x + 7) \\
&= - (e^{x^{2}}(4x^{3} - 6x^{2} - 8x + 7))/((1 - 2x)^{3}(x - 1)^{4})
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8cf6e625-669a-5fda-b756-e1ce091eaa93" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6090 :tutorial/title "Using Logarithms to Differentiate a Quotient"} :step/id #uuid "2141558f-a6d2-515d-902a-620581d72401" :step/math-academy-id 37041 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065208}}] :activity/title "Further Logarithmic Differentiation" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186064435} {:db/id 17592186065206 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065396 :tutorial/content "When a function $y=y(x)$ contains complex products, quotients, or radicals, we can use logarithmic differentiation to find the derivative $y'(x)$.

For example, consider the following function:

$$
y = x^2 \cdot 2^x
$$

Our goal is to find $y'(x)$. To do this, we will use the product rule for logarithms, namely

$$
\ln(a b)= \ln a + \ln b

We differentiate our function by following four steps.

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the product and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ln y &= \ln (x^{2} \cdot 2^{x}) \\
\ln y &= \ln (x^{2}) + \ln (2^{x}) \\
\ln y &= 2\ln x + x\ln 2

$$

**Step 2.** Next, we differentiate both sides of our equation using implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\ln y) &= \frac{d}{dx}(2\ln x + x\ln 2) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot y^{′} &= 2 \cdot (\ln x)^{′} + (x)^{′} \cdot \ln (2) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot y^{′} &= 2 \cdot \frac{1}{x} + 1 \cdot \ln (2) \\
\frac{y^{′}}{y} &= \frac{2}{x} + \ln 2
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Then, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= y(\frac{2}{x} + \ln 2)
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for

$$
y =x^2\cdot 2^x{:}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= x^{2} \cdot 2^{x}(\frac{2}{x} + \ln 2) \\
&= x \cdot 2^{x + 1} + x^{2} \cdot 2^{x}\ln 2
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1895a7f3-5ba4-5a31-85b3-6a7b050b307c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6088 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "caef414d-4f2a-5504-9b92-39a03d2f3c8f" :step/math-academy-id 37035 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065207}} {:db/id 17592186065396 :tutorial/content "When a function $y=y(x)$ contains complex products, quotients, or radicals, we can use logarithmic differentiation to find the derivative $y'(x)$.

For example, consider the following function:

$$
y = x^2 \cdot 2^x
$$

Our goal is to find $y'(x)$. To do this, we will use the product rule for logarithms, namely

$$
\ln(a b)= \ln a + \ln b
$$

We differentiate our function by following four steps.

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the product and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ln y &= \ln (x^{2} \cdot 2^{x}) \\
\ln y &= \ln (x^{2}) + \ln (2^{x}) \\
\ln y &= 2\ln x + x\ln 2
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Next, we differentiate both sides of our equation using implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\ln y) &= \frac{d}{dx}(2\ln x + x\ln 2) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot y^{′} &= 2 \cdot (\ln x)^{′} + (x)^{′} \cdot \ln (2) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot y^{′} &= 2 \cdot \frac{1}{x} + 1 \cdot \ln (2) \\
\frac{y^{′}}{y} &= \frac{2}{x} + \ln 2
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Then, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= y(\frac{2}{x} + \ln 2)
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for

$$
y =x^2\cdot 2^x{:}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= x^{2} \cdot 2^{x}(\frac{2}{x} + \ln 2) \\
&= x \cdot 2^{x + 1} + x^{2} \cdot 2^{x}\ln 2
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1895a7f3-5ba4-5a31-85b3-6a7b050b307c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6088 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186065207 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064309 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064146 :question/id #uuid "c24da7ef-0070-5aae-bade-c82ea56476ba" :question/math-academy-id "e-9845"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7613eee3-a281-57cb-bc47-3b1594920bd1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048773} {:db/id 17592186050375}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064655} {:db/id 17592186064662}] :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating a Product"} :step/id #uuid "b6a516b4-d0c4-5ec7-8f7e-12edd0e85c51" :step/math-academy-id 37036 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065210}} {:db/id 17592186065210 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065397 :tutorial/content "In cases where we wish to differentiate a quotient of functions

$$
y = f(x) = \dfrac{g(x)}{h(x)}
$$

we can apply the quotient rule for logarithms:

$$
\ln \left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right) = \ln a - \ln b
$$

For example, let's compute $y'$, where the function $y$ is given by

$$
y = \dfrac {e^{x^2}}{(1-2x)^2(x-1)^3}
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ln y &= \ln ((e^{x^{2}})/((1 - 2x)^{2}(x - 1)^{3})) \\
\ln y &= \ln (e^{x^{2}}) - \ln ((1 - 2x)^{2}) - \ln ((x - 1)^{3}) \\
\ln y &= x^{2} - 2\ln (1 - 2x) - 3\ln (x - 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\ln y) &= \frac{d}{dx}(x^{2} - 2\ln (1 - 2x) - 3\ln (x - 1)) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot y^{′} &= 2x - 2 \cdot \frac{1}{1 - 2x} \cdot (-2) - 3 \cdot \frac{1}{x - 1} \\
\frac{y^{′}}{y} &= 2x + \frac{4}{1 - 2x} - \frac{3}{x - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= y(2x + \frac{4}{1 - 2x} - \frac{3}{x - 1})
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute our expression for $y$, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= (e^{x^{2}})/((1 - 2x)^{2}(x - 1)^{3})(2x + \frac{4}{1 - 2x} - \frac{3}{x - 1}) \\
&= (e^{x^{2}})/((1 - 2x)^{2}(x - 1)^{3})((2x(1 - 2x)(x - 1) + 4(x - 1) - 3(1 - 2x))/((1 - 2x)(x - 1))) \\
&= (e^{x^{2}})/((1 - 2x)^{3}(x - 1)^{4})(2x(1 - 2x)(x - 1) + 4(x - 1) - 3(1 - 2x)) \\
&= (e^{x^{2}})/((1 - 2x)^{3}(x - 1)^{4})(-4x^{3} + 6x^{2} + 8x - 7) \\
&= - (e^{x^{2}})/((1 - 2x)^{3}(x - 1)^{4})(4x^{3} - 6x^{2} - 8x + 7) \\
&= - (e^{x^{2}}(4x^{3} - 6x^{2} - 8x + 7))/((1 - 2x)^{3}(x - 1)^{4})
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8cf6e625-669a-5fda-b756-e1ce091eaa93" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6090 :tutorial/title "Using Logarithms to Differentiate a Quotient"} :step/id #uuid "2141558f-a6d2-515d-902a-620581d72401" :step/math-academy-id 37041 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065208}} {:db/id 17592186065208 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064310 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064147 :question/id #uuid "7db11c8c-344b-5d87-a8ae-3b006e5bd92b" :question/math-academy-id "e-9846"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "71dd9228-4b05-54d9-aeb2-3bdabf89e0e9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049079} {:db/id 17592186050542}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064653} {:db/id 17592186064663}] :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating a Quotient"} :step/id #uuid "57a60273-bc58-5aff-8dcd-d7139782aa2a" :step/math-academy-id 37037 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065209}} {:db/id 17592186065209 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064311 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064148 :question/id #uuid "e0cec84d-96cf-5fed-ba05-a5cfc57841a1" :question/math-academy-id "e-9847"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c6005f9a-3eba-5f8d-909d-894d9cd24d12" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050208} {:db/id 17592186050496} {:db/id 17592186050887} {:db/id 17592186050894}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064652} {:db/id 17592186064654} {:db/id 17592186233441}] :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating a Radical Expression"} :step/id #uuid "8850f22e-33ee-545a-8f5e-4dc37bda3b30" :step/math-academy-id 37038} {:db/id 17592186065397 :tutorial/content "In cases where we wish to differentiate a quotient of functions

The graph $z=f(x,y)$ is shown above. What are the global maximum points of the function?" :question/worked-solution "First, we recall the following definitions:

- The global maximum of a function is the largest value it attains on its domain. There can only be (at most) one global maximum.

- A global maximum point is a point $(x,y,z)$ where a function reaches a global maximum. There can be zero, one, or many global maximum points.

In other words, we can take a neighborhood of $(x,y)$-values such that the point $(x,y,f(x,y))$ is the highest point on the graph in the neighborhood.

Such neighborhoods exist for the points $B$ and $D.$ Hence $B$ and $D$ are local maxima.

given by

$$
f(x)≈1+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ 3 & -6\end{aligned}](x-a).
$$

Given that the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-9,$ what type of point is $a?$" :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

The quadratic Taylor expansion of a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ about $x=a\in {R}^{n}$ given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a).
$$

Since the quadratic Taylor expansion of $f$ has no $(x-a)$ term, we can conclude that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ Hence, $a$ is a critical point of $f.$

Finally, notice that both the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & =-3<0 \\ {\lambda }_{2} & =-9<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix is negative definite. Therefore, $a$ is a local maximum of $f.$"} {:db/id 17592186401419 :question/id #uuid "c9ce8c10-95e8-5421-97ed-611d96bbf7c9" :question/math-academy-id "q-163771"} {:db/id 17592186434751 :question/id "0a177390-6525-5d0c-8721-f7f75db39408" :topic/math-academy-id 1945} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125485 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125816 :tutorial/content "So, given a stationary critical point $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ of a function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R},$ how do we classify it?

One way is to consider the Taylor expansion of $f$ about $\mathbf{a}{:}$

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{a}) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \cdots
$$

Since $\mathbf{a}$ is a stationary point, we have $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf 0^T.$ This gives

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{a})  + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \cdots.
$$

Let's assume that $\mathbf x$ is close to $\mathbf a,$ $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0,$ and that the terms of cubic order and higher are sufficiently small. Then, we have

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) \approx f(\mathbf{a})  + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}).
$$

Recall that $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is an $n \times n$ *symmetric* matrix. Thus, the term

$$
(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
$$

is a *quadratic form*.

Therefore, we note the following:

- If $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is positive definite, this quadratic form is always positive, and

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) > 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(\mathbf{x}) > f(\mathbf{a})
$$

for all $\mathbf{x}$ sufficiently close to $\mathbf{a}.$ Hence, $\mathbf{a}$ is a local *minimum*.

- If $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is negative definite, this quadratic form is always negative, and

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) < 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(\mathbf{x}) < f(\mathbf{a})
$$

for all $\mathbf{x}$ sufficiently close to $\mathbf{a}.$ Hence, $\mathbf{a}$ is a local *maximum.*

- If this quadratic form is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $\mathbf{a}$ is a saddle point.

The assumption $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0$ is important. If $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) =0,$ then the quadratic form is zero along some line through $\mathbf a$ or zero *everywhere* in a neighborhood of $\mathbf a.$ In such cases, we cannot ignore the higher-order terms and must use another method to classify the critical point.

In the work that follows, we will only consider cases where $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3cedcd0c-77c7-5789-b76d-7ae3307c237b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4263 :tutorial/title "Classifying Local Extrema Using Taylor Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "f3f90cb9-acd8-5630-859d-3bd37e502189" :step/math-academy-id 25915 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125645}} {:db/id 17592186125486 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125817 :tutorial/content "Recall that the *derivative* of a multivariable function $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ is given by the matrix

![](images/b5/b5dfe5fbad89ef3c6231dafe40d719be1faf007f782342abd6475756eda97b1e.svg)

Analogously with functions of one variable, we have the following definitions:

- A point $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ is a **critical point** of $f$ if $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ or does not exist.

- Critical points where $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ are known as **stationary points.**

The local extrema of a function $f$ occur at the critical points. So, we can find the local extrema of $f$ by determining the stationary points *and* the points where $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf x)$ does not exist and classify them accordingly (we'll discuss how to do this shortly). 

Not all of the solutions of $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ give rise to local extrema! Solutions to $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ that *do not* give rise to local extreme values are called **saddle points**.

For example, consider the hyperbolic paraboloid 

$$
z = f(x,y) = y^2-x^2
$$

whose graph is shown below.

![](images/ce/cea092da684db6b055c78369fcb987c3577a027ef0d8f03d598e115e85775ff5.png)

It's easy to check that $\boldsymbol f'(0,0) = \mathbf 0^T,$ and so $(0,0)$ is a stationary point of $f.$ This point is a saddle point. Note that the surface curves up in one direction (the red curve) and down in a different direction (the green curve), resembling a horse riding saddle.

In any neighborhood of a saddle point $\mathbf a,$ there are points $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{x}'$ such that $\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{x}'-\mathbf{a}$ are orthogonal and they satisfy

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf a) >0 \quad \textrm{and} \quad f(\mathbf{x}') - f(\mathbf a) <0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "60d15795-6c7a-5ec9-806d-625f5d8c5c85" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4264 :tutorial/title "Saddle Points"} :step/id #uuid "42eecd67-0de9-5101-84f7-5ef560683d60" 44846 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125486}} {:db/id 17592186125628 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125873 :tutorial/content "Now, recall the definition of local extrema for single-variable functions:

- A function $f(x)$ has a local minimum at $x=a$ if $f(x) \geq f(a)$ for all $x$-values in a neighborhood of $a.$

- A function $f(x)$ has a local maximum at $x=a$ if $f(x) \leq f(a)$ for all $x$-values in a neighborhood of $a.$

On the function's graph, a local minimum is the lowest point of a valley, and a local maximum is the highest point of a peak.

![](images/ba/ba5be082363bd963514baa6b1a777f02098d53a3b0a80ddc2fad231e4669ebd7.png)

We can generalize the concept of local extrema to multivariable functions $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ as follows:

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a local minimum at the point $\mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \geq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x}$ in a neighborhood of $\mathbf{a}.$

![](images/74/74d04165fd3bd5cd24ae82351bbf840e7d549b272c3deea16671dbfcd40bc75a.png)

For the points $A$ and $B,$ we can take neighborhoods of the $(x,y)$-values at these points such that $A$ and $B$ are the lowest points on the graph in these neighborhoods. Hence, they are local minima.

Similarly, for the points $C$ and $D,$ we can take neighborhoods of the $(x,y)$-values at these points such that $C$ and $D$ are the highest points on the graph in these neighborhoods. Hence, they are local maxima.

**Note**: For the point $E,$ there are points $(x,y)$ in the surrounding regions such that $f(x_E,y_E) = f(x,y).$ However, since the definition of local extrema is non-strict, $f(\mathbf{x}) \geq f(\mathbf{a})$ or $f(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{a})$, the point $E$ satisfies the conditions for a local minimum *and* a local maximum.

Finally, the points $F$ and $G$ are neither local minima nor local maxima. - Similarly, the maximum value reached by the function is $f(x,y) = 2,$ so the global maximum is $2.$ The function reaches this value at $(x,y) = (1,1).$ Therefore the global maximum point is $(1,1,2).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c6c71de7-b70c-5b7f-a566-143fd897ff59" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7753 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d367e806-9c4c-5d98-bc43-97c56882eee8" :step/math-academy-id 44876 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125625}} {:db/id 17592186125485 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125816 :tutorial/content "So, given a stationary critical point $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ of a function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R},$ how do we classify it?

One way is to consider the Taylor expansion of $f$ about $\mathbf{a}{:}$

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{a}) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \cdots
$$

Since $\mathbf{a}$ is a stationary point, we have $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf 0^T.$ This gives

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{a})  + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \cdots.
$$

Let's assume that $\mathbf x$ is close to $\mathbf a,$ $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0,$ and that the terms of cubic order and higher are sufficiently small. Then, we have

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) \approx f(\mathbf{a})  + \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
$$

which we can rewrite as

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}).
$$

Recall that $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is an $n \times n$ *symmetric* matrix. Thus, the term

$$
(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
$$

is a *quadratic form*.

Therefore, we note the following:

- If $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is positive definite, this quadratic form is always positive, and

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) > 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(\mathbf{x}) > f(\mathbf{a})
$$

for all $\mathbf{x}$ sufficiently close to $\mathbf{a}.$ Hence, $\mathbf{a}$ is a local *minimum*.

- If $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is negative definite, this quadratic form is always negative, and

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \dfrac12(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) < 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(\mathbf{x}) < f(\mathbf{a})
$$

for all $\mathbf{x}$ sufficiently close to $\mathbf{a}.$ Hence, $\mathbf{a}$ is a local *maximum.*

- If this quadratic form is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $\mathbf{a}$ is a saddle point.

The assumption $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0$ is important. If $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) =0,$ then the quadratic form is zero along some line through $\mathbf a$ or zero *everywhere* in a neighborhood of $\mathbf a.$ In such cases, we cannot ignore the higher-order terms and must use another method to classify the critical point.

In the work that follows, we will only consider cases where $\det\left(\boldsymbol f''(\mathbf a)\right) \neq 0.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3cedcd0c-77c7-5789-b76d-7ae3307c237b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4263 :tutorial/title "Classifying Local Extrema Using Taylor Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "f3f90cb9-acd8-5630-859d-3bd37e502189" :step/math-academy-id 25915 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125645}} {:db/id 17592186125816 :tutorial/content "So, given a stationary critical point $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ of a function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R},$ how do we classify it?

Analogously with functions of one variable, we have the following definitions:

- A point $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ is a **critical point** of $f$ if $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ or does not exist.

Not all of the solutions of $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ give rise to local extrema! Solutions to $\boldsymbol f'(\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0^T$ that *do not* give rise to local extreme values are called **saddle points**.

$$

$$

- A function $f(x)$ over the domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ has a global minimum point at $x=a$ if $f(x) \geq f(a)$ for all $x \in D.$

- A function $f(x)$ over the domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ has a global maximum point at $x=a$ if $f(x) \leq f(a)$ for all $x \in D.$

On the function's graph, the global minimum and maximum are the lowest and highest points, respectively.

![](images/63/633526565293f480a6a5fc45b87a70d38e946ae0f72a925f0074776e201a43a4.png)

We can generalize this concept to multivariable functions $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R.$

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a **global minimum point** at $\mathbf x = \mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \geq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x} \in D.$ The value $f(\mathbf{a})$ is the **global minimum** of the function, the smallest value the function attains on its domain.

- A multivariable function $f(\mathbf{x})$ with domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ has a **global maximum point** at $\mathbf x = \mathbf{a} \in D$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{a})$ for all points $\mathbf{x} \in D.$ The value $f(\mathbf{a})$ is the **global maximum** of the function, the largest value the function attains on its domain.

In particular, for a function $f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R},$ the global minimum and maximum are the lowest and highest points on the graph $z=f(x,y),$ respectively.

![](images/de/de4cfc96fdce210430291999e5997f4a0c39ed1fbe63c3848b61508ca3f04114.png)

For the function shown above:

- The minimum value reached by the function is $f(x,y) = -2,$ so the global minimum is $-2,$ The function reaches this value at $(x,y) = (1,-1).$ Therefore the global minimum point is $(1,-1,-2).$

- Similarly, the maximum value reached by the function is $f(x,y) = 2,$ so the global maximum is $2.$ The function reaches this value at $(x,y) = (1,1).$ Therefore the global maximum point is $(1,1,2).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c6c71de7-b70c-5b7f-a566-143fd897ff59" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7753 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186125885 :tutorial/content "To summarize, the point $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is a stationary point of the function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ if $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf 0^T,$ and we can classify $\mathbf{a}$ as follows:

- if $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is positive definite, then $\mathbf{a}$ is a local minimum

- if $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is negative definite, then $\mathbf{a}$ is a local maximum

- if $\boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a})$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $\mathbf{a}$ is a saddle point" :tutorial/id #uuid "ab23ca4b-1bff-5c96-a4d2-62b72b8adff2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7852 :tutorial/title "A Summary of Key Results"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046660} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186445202} :activity/id #uuid "632f0c8c-4357-5396-aad3-4401d3471d8c" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049676 :topic/id #uuid "0a177390-6525-5d0c-8721-f7f75db39408" :topic/math-academy-id 1945} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186445199 :step/content {:db/id 17592186367874 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "99f22169-b8a2-5fb3-aca1-3e5599415ad8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "local maximum" :db/id 17592186367876} {:answer/id #uuid "abbaa7f2-5259-5b5a-bebd-07f255b181e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "inconclusive" :db/id 17592186367877} {:answer/id #uuid "f674340e-9bc4-5748-9997-f0404db95ca2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "not a critical point" :db/id 17592186367878} {:answer/id #uuid "383240c1-34bf-5387-adaf-b9355e4cf27e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "local minimum" :db/id 17592186367879} {:answer/id #uuid "0e483432-9f14-537e-b0dd-61a175cc1645" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "saddle point" :db/id 17592186367880}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367876} :answer-field/id #uuid "be669623-0526-55a8-9e58-06217378cfec" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367875}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "1f0502ee-0a83-5915-919b-cb8a0333bfec" :question/math-academy-id "q-163775" :question/problem "The quadratic Taylor approximation of the function $f(x)$ about $x=a\in {R}^{2}$ is given by

$$

$$

Given that the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-9,$ what type of point is $a?$" :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

The quadratic Taylor expansion of a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ about $x=a\in {R}^{n}$ given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a).
$$

Since the quadratic Taylor expansion of $f$ has no $(x-a)$ term, we can conclude that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ Hence, $a$ is a critical point of $f.$

Finally, notice that both the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & =-3<0 \\ {\lambda }_{2} & =-9<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix is negative definite. $$
f(x)≈1+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ 3 & -6\end{aligned}](x-a).
$$

Given that the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-9,$ what type of point is $a?$" :question/worked-solution "The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

The quadratic Taylor expansion of a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ about $x=a\in {R}^{n}$ given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a).
$$

Since the quadratic Taylor expansion of $f$ has no $(x-a)$ term, we can conclude that ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ Hence, $a$ is a critical point of $f.$

Finally, notice that both the eigenvalues of ${f}^{″}(a)$ are negative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & =-3<0 \\ {\lambda }_{2} & =-9<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix is negative definite. - The global minimum of a function is the smallest value it attains on its domain. There can only be (at most) one global minimum.

- A global minimum point is a point $(x,y,z)$ where a function reaches a global minimum. There can be zero, one, or many global minimum points.

For our function, the minimum value reached by the function is $f(x,y)=-2.$ Therefore, the global minimum is $-2.$ The function reaches this value when $(x,y)=(1,1),$ so the global minimum point is $(1,1,-2).$

Let's work out the value of $-5+7$ using both methods.

**Method 1 - Picturing a Number Line**

When we add, we move to the right on the number line.

So, to add $7$ to $-5,$ we start at $-5$ on a number line and move $7$ spaces to the right.

![](images/e6/e6f99b09208d09824dc7c4e6dfaafdc0e20feb7fde00f821a57a70d79196936d.png)

 

When we do this, we land at $2.$ Therefore, $-5+7 =2.$

**Method 2 - Subtraction in Reverse**

Adding a positive number to a negative number is like *subtraction in reverse*. To turn the addition into a subtraction, we must switch the numbers around.

So, to work out ${\color{red}{-5}} + {\color{blue}{7}},$ we can switch the numbers around to get 
$\,{\color{blue}{7}} {\color{red}{\,-\,5}} =2.$

We're allowed to swap the numbers because addition is **commutative**, which means the order in which we add two numbers does not matter." :tutorial/id #uuid "fea61476-1945-5134-8063-3e50b2865f8f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8382 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1c01112c-13ce-5b10-8825-cd205fd87939" :step/math-academy-id 74975 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065277}} {:db/id 17592186065277 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064354 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063965 :question/id #uuid "4d61f8ae-cf47-5aa7-96f8-770a232509ea" :question/math-academy-id "e-13380"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "09d49af8-8aed-5434-bbf4-12c90c658fc0" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048911}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064487} {:db/id 17592186064555} {:db/id 17592186445414}] :knowledge-point/title "Adding a Positive Number to a Negative Number"} :step/id #uuid "d317273f-64d9-5382-91e1-beb5ef25c23c" :step/math-academy-id 74976 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065278}} {:db/id 17592186065278 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064355 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063966 :question/id #uuid "a92db588-62a8-5a19-8420-a38d25dd9088" :question/math-academy-id "e-13381"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b20f6b97-6531-5ece-a1d0-4d25d4895dab" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048207}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064486} {:db/id 17592186064760} {:db/id 17592186064761} {:db/id 17592186445412} {:db/id 17592186445413} {:db/id 17592186445415}] :knowledge-point/title "Adding a Positive Decimal to a Negative Decimal"} :step/id #uuid "fdbb7f5d-0de1-5533-a248-8d52ffb6de29" :step/math-academy-id 74979 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065279}} {:db/id 17592186065279 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065431 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to calculate $-\dfrac 1 3 + \dfrac 5 3.$

Since both fractions have a common denominator of $3,$ we can combine them to form one fraction:

 

$$
-\dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{5}{3} =\dfrac{-1+5}{3}
$$

To compute the numerator, we can use either method that we've learned.

**Method 1 - Picturing a Number Line**

To add $5$ to $-1,$ we start at $-1$ on a number line and move $5$ spaces to the right.

![](images/63/632e4bcce5b619f9a5c4dfb2c414a33da0e9567b7b4d8b15adb439da1b3dd88d.png)

We end up at $4.$ So $-1+5=4,$ and therefore

$$
\dfrac{-1+5}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}.
$$

**Method 2 - Subtraction in Reverse**

We can swap the order of the numbers in the numerator and then compute the resulting subtraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-1+5}{3}=\frac{5-1}{3}=\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that $-\dfrac1 3 + \dfrac 5 3 = \dfrac{4}{3}.$

**Note:** If two fractions have different denominators, we need to put them over a common denominator *first* and *then* subtract!" :tutorial/id #uuid "9522d6a9-a066-57d7-bf8a-e4baf0467548" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8383 :tutorial/title "Adding a Positive Fraction to a Negative Fraction"} :step/id #uuid "51a3f9a7-44e9-5617-afa0-b6145e79910d" :step/math-academy-id 74983 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065280}} {:db/id 17592186065280 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064356 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186063967 :question/id #uuid "a287913a-827a-56fa-8bbf-5f716dff277e" :question/math-academy-id "e-13382"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "169a836e-5209-53a1-bda9-0542b044819d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048639}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064464} {:db/id 17592186064465} {:db/id 17592186064488} {:db/id 17592186445410} {:db/id 17592186445411}] :knowledge-point/title "Adding a Positive Fraction to a Negative Fraction"} :step/id #uuid "fb6f62cc-a440-5782-82f3-8987d7d10530" :step/math-academy-id 74984}] :activity/title "Adding a Positive Number to a Negative Number" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186064420} {:db/id 17592186065276 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065430 :tutorial/content "There are two ways to add a positive number to a negative number. ![](images/e6/e6f99b09208d09824dc7c4e6dfaafdc0e20feb7fde00f821a57a70d79196936d.png)

 

When we do this, we land at $2.$ Therefore, $-5+7 =2.$

**Method 2 - Subtraction in Reverse**

Adding a positive number to a negative number is like *subtraction in reverse*. To turn the addition into a subtraction, we must switch the numbers around.

So, to work out ${\color{red}{-5}} + {\color{blue}{7}},$ we can switch the numbers around to get 
$\,{\color{blue}{7}} {\color{red}{\,-\,5}} =2.$

We're allowed to swap the numbers because addition is **commutative**, which means the order in which we add two numbers does not matter." :tutorial/id #uuid "fea61476-1945-5134-8063-3e50b2865f8f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8382 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1c01112c-13ce-5b10-8825-cd205fd87939" :step/math-academy-id 74975 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065277}} {:db/id 17592186065430 :tutorial/content "There are two ways to add a positive number to a negative number. Since both fractions have a common denominator of $3,$ we can combine them to form one fraction:

 

$$
-\dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{5}{3} =\dfrac{-1+5}{3}
$$

To compute the numerator, we can use either method that we've learned.

**Method 1 - Picturing a Number Line**

To add $5$ to $-1,$ we start at $-1$ on a number line and move $5$ spaces to the right.

![](images/63/632e4bcce5b619f9a5c4dfb2c414a33da0e9567b7b4d8b15adb439da1b3dd88d.png)

We end up at $4.$ So $-1+5=4,$ and therefore

$$
\dfrac{-1+5}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}.
$$

**Method 2 - Subtraction in Reverse**

We can swap the order of the numbers in the numerator and then compute the resulting subtraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-1+5}{3}=\frac{5-1}{3}=\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that $-\dfrac1 3 + \dfrac 5 3 = \dfrac{4}{3}.$

**Note:** If two fractions have different denominators, we need to put them over a common denominator *first* and *then* subtract!" :tutorial/id #uuid "9522d6a9-a066-57d7-bf8a-e4baf0467548" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8383 :tutorial/title "Adding a Positive Fraction to a Negative Fraction"} :step/id #uuid "51a3f9a7-44e9-5617-afa0-b6145e79910d" :step/math-academy-id 74983 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065280}} {:db/id 17592186065431 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to calculate $-\dfrac 1 3 + \dfrac 5 3.$

:topic/math-academy-id 2174} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134590 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135180 :tutorial/content "To **square** a number means to multiply that number by itself. 

For example, to "square $3$", we need to multiply $3$ by $3.$ We write the "square of $3$" as $3^2,$ so we have

$$
3^2 = 3 \cdot 3 = {\color{blue}9}.
$$

We would then say that "the square of $3$ is $9$". We could also say "$3$ squared equals $9$".

The number $\color{blue}2$ in the expression $3^{\color{blue}2}$ is called the **power** or **exponent**.

The act of squaring a number can be represented geometrically. For example, let's start by representing the number $3$ with the following collection of three items:

![](images/4a/4a4dbb46401052829138bddc1653ae843babf4c5cfb6ba9fc40ca29ede99bd70.png)

Then we can picture $3^2$ by creating a square with length and height both equal to $3\mathbin{:}$

![](images/cc/cc343eafb463e25ab429bafbc06216dad73037e5a02a2be9adfe046629636013.png)

There are $9$ items in total in our square, indicating that $3^2 = 9.$

The first few basic squares are shown below:

| $1^2=1 \cdot 1={\color{blue}1}$ | $2^2=2 \cdot 2={\color{blue}4}$ | $3^2=3 \cdot 3={\color{blue}9}$ | $4^2=4 \cdot 4={\color{blue}16}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ![](images/ce/ce5db07809eb56891f31ac7fb0257edb42bd650f00c51c25857b02d1333165ad.png) | ![](images/61/6113e94a28fc50c7f1fe77ddf082d28d543aa9e2b6e65f82e8623a89f624f7db.png) | ![](images/cc/cc343eafb463e25ab429bafbc06216dad73037e5a02a2be9adfe046629636013.png) | ![](images/7d/7d56b21746fa8a0053fa32b6c2bc6d9393e13459cb65473e64589cc2f6a01ad3.png) |

The squares of our usual counting numbers are called **square numbers** or **perfect squares**. We can write them as follows:

$$
1^2, 2^2, 3^2, 4^2, 5^2, 6^2, \ldots \qquad \text{or} \qquad {\color{blue}1}, {\color{blue}4}, {\color{blue}9}, {\color{blue}16}, {\color{blue}25}, {\color{blue}36}, \ldots
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "31cd70b9-a231-5c24-b6f4-1a3e714912b6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8102 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "532d5ecd-c046-546b-906b-aa64daf1f6f9" :step/math-academy-id 151107 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134591}} {:db/id 17592186134591 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133734 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133507 :question/id #uuid "62c086b3-028f-528b-acd5-7bdc204dcb23" :question/math-academy-id "e-12960"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a6f6a3fd-67df-5671-aa5d-08471b2ce1fb" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048924}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134327} {:db/id 17592186134405} {:db/id 17592186443073} {:db/id 17592186443077} {:db/id 17592186443083} {:db/id 17592186443085} {:db/id 17592186443088}] :knowledge-point/title "Squaring Positive Whole Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "0708b802-2bb7-5823-be5b-b14cb353d3fe" :step/math-academy-id 151108 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134592}} {:db/id 17592186134592 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133735 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133508 :question/id #uuid "4a393145-3e63-532b-a288-775fbc7acd15" :question/math-academy-id "e-12961"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "eece577d-72b8-5a0d-89fd-1cfa63bf73fb" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049253}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134325} {:db/id 17592186134509} {:db/id 17592186443072} {:db/id 17592186443074} {:db/id 17592186443079} {:db/id 17592186443082} {:db/id 17592186443084}] :knowledge-point/title "Squaring Fractions"} :step/id #uuid "70765661-2016-5e64-9ab9-d709f8ecd73b" :step/math-academy-id 151111 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134593}} {:db/id 17592186134593 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135181 :tutorial/content "The squares of negative numbers are always positive because a negative times a negative is positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-)\,\cdot \,(-)\,=\,(+)\end{aligned}
$$

Some squares of negative numbers are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)^{2}\,=\,(-1)\cdot (-1) & \,=\,1 \\ (-2)^{2}\,=\,(-2)\cdot (-2) & \,=\,4 \\ (-3)^{2}\,=\,(-3)\cdot (-3) & \,=\,9 \\ (-4)^{2}\,=\,(-4)\cdot (-4) & \,=\,16 \\ (-5)^{2}\,=\,(-5)\cdot (-5) & \,=\,25\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch Out!** When squaring negative numbers, the parentheses are important! 

Consider the following squared quantity:

$$
-3^2
$$

This is *not* the same as $(-3)^2$. Instead, this is a shorthand way of writing

$$
(-1) \cdot 3^2.
$$

According to the order of operations, we should square $3$ *first* and *then* multiply by $-1.$ Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{3}^{2} & =(-1)\cdot {3}^{2} \\  & =(-1)\cdot 9 \\  & =-9\end{aligned}

The number $\color{blue}2$ in the expression $3^{\color{blue}2}$ is called the **power** or **exponent**.

The act of squaring a number can be represented geometrically. For example, let's start by representing the number $3$ with the following collection of three items:

![](images/4a/4a4dbb46401052829138bddc1653ae843babf4c5cfb6ba9fc40ca29ede99bd70.png)

![](images/cc/cc343eafb463e25ab429bafbc06216dad73037e5a02a2be9adfe046629636013.png)

There are $9$ items in total in our square, indicating that $3^2 = 9.$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-)\,\cdot \,(-)\,=\,(+)\end{aligned}
$$

Some squares of negative numbers are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)^{2}\,=\,(-1)\cdot (-1) & \,=\,1 \\ (-2)^{2}\,=\,(-2)\cdot (-2) & \,=\,4 \\ (-3)^{2}\,=\,(-3)\cdot (-3) & \,=\,9 \\ (-4)^{2}\,=\,(-4)\cdot (-4) & \,=\,16 \\ (-5)^{2}\,=\,(-5)\cdot (-5) & \,=\,25\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch Out!** When squaring negative numbers, the parentheses are important! 

Consider the following squared quantity:

$$
-3^2
$$

This is *not* the same as $(-3)^2$. Instead, this is a shorthand way of writing

$$
(-1) \cdot 3^2.
$$

According to the order of operations, we should square $3$ *first* and *then* multiply by $-1.$ Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{3}^{2} & =(-1)\cdot {3}^{2} \\  & =(-1)\cdot 9 \\  & =-9\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "38064eee-d6b6-5557-881a-ed03baadeed7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8103 :tutorial/title "Squaring Negative Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "4aa26ed8-8e70-561f-a525-88bd5896de45" :step/math-academy-id 151114 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134594}} {:db/id 17592186135181 :tutorial/content "The squares of negative numbers are always positive because a negative times a negative is positive:

A graphic designer is animating a circle in such a way that the area of the circle increases at a rate of $7\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$ How fast is the radius of the circle increasing at the moment when the radius is $1\text{ cm}?$" :question/worked-solution "In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=1,$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=7\pi .$

To start, let's write down the area formula for the circle and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=7\pi $ and $r=1,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}7\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi (1) \\ 7\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =3.5.\end{aligned}
$$

"Suppose we're told that the radius of a circle is **growing at a rate of $2\,\textrm{cm}$ every second**, as shown below.

![](images/27/27d0543834333202411a9700401b7e33329a255c7103c9f2ebe394d8c1cf694b.png)

If the radius of the circle is growing, then its area is also increasing. How do we calculate the **rate at which the area is increasing**?

The rate at which the area is changing can be expressed using a derivative:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t}
$$

Here, $A$ is the area of the circle, measured in $\textrm{cm}^2,$ and $t$ is the time in seconds. 

We know that the area is related to the radius $r$ as

$$
A = \pi r^2.
$$

Differentiating the above using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r\end{aligned}
$$

Since the radius of a circle is growing at a rate of $2\,\textrm{cm}$ every second, we have $\dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt} = 2 \, \textrm{cm}.$ Substituting this information, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =2\cdot 2\pi r=4\pi r\,{\text{cm}}^{2}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

And, that's it, we're done! 

If we want to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t}$ at a particular moment, we substitute the value of $r$ at that moment into the above. So, for example, if we want to compute $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t}$ at the moment when $r=6\,\textrm{cm},$ we plug this into the above and get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = 4\pi \cdot 6 = 24\pi\,\textrm{cm}^2/\textrm{s}.

17592186065317 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065384 :tutorial/content "Suppose we're told that the radius of a circle is **growing at a rate of $2\,\textrm{cm}$ every second**, as shown below.

![](images/27/27d0543834333202411a9700401b7e33329a255c7103c9f2ebe394d8c1cf694b.png)

If the radius of the circle is growing, then its area is also increasing. How do we calculate the **rate at which the area is increasing**?

The rate at which the area is changing can be expressed using a derivative:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t}
$$

Here, $A$ is the area of the circle, measured in $\textrm{cm}^2,$ and $t$ is the time in seconds. 

We know that the area is related to the radius $r$ as

$$
A = \pi r^2.
$$

Differentiating the above using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\pi r\end{aligned}
$$

Since the radius of a circle is growing at a rate of $2\,\textrm{cm}$ every second, we have $\dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt} = 2 \, \textrm{cm}.$ Substituting this information, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =2\cdot 2\pi r=4\pi r\,{\text{cm}}^{2}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

And, that's it, we're done! 

If we want to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t}$ at a particular moment, we substitute the value of $r$ at that moment into the above. So, for example, if we want to compute $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t}$ at the moment when $r=6\,\textrm{cm},$ we plug this into the above and get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = 4\pi \cdot 6 = 24\pi\,\textrm{cm}^2/\textrm{s}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6925e269-127a-5cf1-8116-aa809d1cf42f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 488 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "2f58c76e-8d14-575a-b5de-62cc2003eb38" :step/math-academy-id 906 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065319}} {:db/id 17592186065384 :tutorial/content "Suppose we're told that the radius of a circle is **growing at a rate of $2\,\textrm{cm}$ every second**, as shown below.

:step/content {:db/id 17592186075060 :tutorial/content "A **triangle** is a geometric shape that consists of three points connected by three line segments, as shown below.

![](images/06/0668279b79482db2fd78116a244bba8e28d3771f88d2e28fb4b6a62387f9d8fd.png)

For this triangle,

- the line segments $\overline{AB}$, $\overline{BC}$ and $\overline{CA}$ are the **sides** of the triangle,

- the points $\color{red}A$, $\color{red}B$ and $\color{red}C$ are the **vertices** of the triangle,

- the angles $\angle{A}$, $\angle{B}$ and $\angle{C}$ formed by the sides are called the **interior angles** of the triangle.

To denote a triangle, we use the symbol $\boldsymbol{\triangle}$ and list its vertices (in any order). So, the above diagram shows us 

$$
\triangle ABC.
$$

It can be shown that all triangles have the following property:

*The sum of the measures of the interior angles of any triangle is always equal to $180^\circ.$*

For example, in $\triangle ABC$ shown above, the interior angle theorem tells us that

$$
m\angle{A} + m\angle{B} + m\angle{C} = 180^\circ .
$$

Therefore, if we know the measures of two angles in a triangle, we can calculate the value of the other." :tutorial/id #uuid "96cce37a-34b0-5808-afbe-f145cca9fa52" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9135 $$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(x-1)}^{2} & =11 \\ {(x-1)}^{2} & =\frac{11}{2} \\ \sqrt{{(x-1)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{11}{2}} \\ |x-1| & =\sqrt{\frac{11}{2}} \\ x-1 & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{11}{2}} \\ x & =1\pm \sqrt{\frac{11}{2}}\end{aligned}

$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(z-2)}^{2}-{2}^{2} & =5 \\ {(z-2)}^{2}-4 & =5 \\ {(z-2)}^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$-2x^2+2x+1 = 0$ in the form $2(x+p)^2=q,$ and hence solve the equation." :question/worked-solution "First, we multiply the equation by $-1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)\cdot (-2{x}^{2}+2x+1) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-2x-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we move the constant term to the right-hand side, factor the coefficient of the quadratic term, and complete the square on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}-2x-1 & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-2x & =1 \\ 2({x}^{2}-x) & =1 \\ 2[{x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}] & =1 \\ 2[{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}] & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we expand the brackets, and write the equation in the required form:

$$
\begin{aligned}2[{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}] & =1 \\ 2{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{2} & =1 \\ 2{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-\dfrac12$ and $q=\dfrac32.$ We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ {(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \sqrt{{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\ |x-\frac{1}{2}| & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ x-\frac{1}{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186184814 :question/id #uuid "219e2398-5583-50ea-9262-64c35b6b5639" :question/math-academy-id "q-60357" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186184192 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3996c79f-9281-5b9d-9b33-8863f10adc33" :knowledge-point/title "Solving a Quadratic Equation With a Negative Leading Coefficient"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "80a960ab-8823-5699-b21e-2a4bb210c0db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "q = \frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186183494} {:answer/id #uuid "a8677aa6-3a74-5438-bfeb-553019eecc2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "q =-\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186183495} {:answer/id #uuid "fceb0dc4-9065-5d6f-a49d-ada0c2e5a7de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "q = \frac{5}{4}" :db/id 17592186183496} {:answer/id #uuid "183dc8e0-12dd-59b1-9d87-bb450ed46d58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "q =-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186183497} {:answer/id #uuid "5ee933bd-186d-5fe7-9ed1-a810b9b27e43" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "q = \frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186183498}] :answer-field/id #uuid "8a373b5f-ae93-59e6-ae47-3ffe140f606a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186183493}] :question/problem "The equation $-5x^{2} + 5x - 1 = 0$ can be written in the form $5(x + p)^{2} = q$. $$

$$

Isolating the perfect square by subtracting $2$ from both sides and then dividing by $(-2),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2(x+1)^{2}+2 & =1 \\ -2(x+1)^{2}+2-2 & =1-2 \\ -2(x+1)^{2} & =-1 \\ (x+1)^{2} & =\frac{(-1)}{(-2)} \\ (x+1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ \sqrt{(x+1)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} \\ |x+1| & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ x+1 & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ x & =-1\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}

$$

Isolating the perfect square by subtracting $24$ from both sides and then dividing by $(-6),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6(y-2)^{2}+24 & =21 \\ -6(y-2)^{2}+24-24 & =21-24 \\ -6(y-2)^{2} & =-3 \\ (y-2)^{2} & =\frac{(-3)}{(-6)} \\ (y-2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ \sqrt{(y-2)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} \\ |y-2| & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ y-2 & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ y & =2\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =\frac{1}{7} \\ \sqrt{(y+3)^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{7}} \\ |y+3| & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}} \\ y+3 & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{7}} \\ y & =-3\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\end{aligned}

*Hint: Use the fact that ${x}^{2}-x+\frac{1}{4}$ is a perfect square.*" :question/worked-solution "Using the hint, we have

$$
{x}^{2}-x+\frac{1}{4}={(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{x}^{2}+4x & =-2 \\ -4({x}^{2}-x) & =-2 \\ -4({x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x) & =-2 \\ -4({x}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}) & =-2 \\ -4[{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}] & =-2 \\ -4[{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}] & =-2 \\ -4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+(-4)(-\frac{1}{4}) & =-2 \\ -4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+1 & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Isolating the perfect square by subtracting $1$ from both sides and then dividing by $(-4),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+1 & =-2 \\ -4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+1-1 & =-2-1 \\ -4{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =-3 \\ {(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{(-3)}{(-4)} \\ {(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \sqrt{{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\ |x-\frac{1}{2}| & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ x-\frac{1}{2} & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ x & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186388841 :question/id #uuid "6cd3a3fd-0ec4-5982-bdba-cd236ee44004" :question/math-academy-id "q-141811"} {:db/id 17592186051081} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid
